verse.text: The book of the origin of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.
verse.note: The same Greek word, genesis, stands here and in verse 18, and most translations hide the link by using two different English words. The opening phrase echoes the Greek of Genesis 2:4 and 5:1, which a reader of the Septuagint would have recognised. Scholars disagree whether verse 1 is a heading for the genealogy alone, for the birth account, or for the whole Gospel; “origin” leaves that open and keeps the repetition.

verse.text: Abraham fathered Isaac, Isaac fathered Jacob, and Jacob fathered Judah and his brothers.
Judah fathered Perez and Zerah by Tamar, Perez fathered Hezron, and Hezron fathered Ram.
verse.note: Ancient Jewish genealogies normally ran through fathers only, so the naming of four women before Mary (Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and Uriah’s wife, Bathsheba) is deliberate. Why these four is debated: all have foreign connections, and each came into the line through an irregular or unexpected union. Either feature, or both, may prepare the reader for Mary.

verse.text: Ram fathered Amminadab, Amminadab fathered Nahshon, and Nahshon fathered Salmon.
Salmon fathered Boaz by Rahab, Boaz fathered Obed by Ruth, and Obed fathered Jesse.
Jesse fathered David the king. David fathered Solomon by Uriah’s wife.
Solomon fathered Rehoboam, Rehoboam fathered Abijah, and Abijah fathered Asaph.
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read Asaph here and Amos in verse 10, where the Old Testament names the kings Asa and Amon; later manuscripts have Asa and Amon. Whether these were accepted variant spellings of the kings’ names or an early confusion with the psalmist Asaph and the prophet Amos is disputed. The translation gives the names as the Greek text has them.

verse.text: Asaph fathered Jehoshaphat, Jehoshaphat fathered Joram, and Joram fathered Uzziah.
Uzziah fathered Jotham, Jotham fathered Ahaz, and Ahaz fathered Hezekiah.
Hezekiah fathered Manasseh, Manasseh fathered Amos, and Amos fathered Josiah.
Josiah fathered Jechoniah and his brothers, at the time of the deportation to Babylon.
After the deportation to Babylon, Jechoniah fathered Shealtiel, and Shealtiel fathered Zerubbabel.
Zerubbabel fathered Abiud, Abiud fathered Eliakim, and Eliakim fathered Azor.
Azor fathered Zadok, Zadok fathered Achim, and Achim fathered Eliud.
Eliud fathered Eleazar, Eleazar fathered Matthan, and Matthan fathered Jacob.
And Jacob fathered Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom was born Jesus, who is called the Messiah.
verse.note: The Greek christos means “anointed” and renders the Hebrew word that gives English “Messiah”, the anointed king Israel expected. Where the word functions as a title, as here and in verse 17, this translation uses “Messiah”; where it is attached to “Jesus” as part of his name, as in verses 1 and 18, it keeps “Christ”. Several modern translations make the same distinction.

verse.text: So all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations, and from David to the deportation to Babylon fourteen generations, and from the deportation to Babylon to the Messiah fourteen generations.
verse.note: The scheme is stylised, not a complete list: comparison with the Old Testament shows that several kings are passed over between Joram and Uzziah, and the verb “fathered” can cover a more distant ancestor. It is often suggested that fourteen was chosen because the Hebrew letters of David’s name add up to that number. This is plausible but cannot be proved.

verse.text: Now the origin of Jesus Christ was like this. When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to be pregnant by the Holy Spirit.

note.traditional: betrothed; engaged; pledged to be married

verse.note: Jewish betrothal was a legally binding contract, not an engagement in the modern sense. It could be ended only by divorce or death, which is why Joseph is already called Mary’s husband and considers divorce. The couple did not yet live together; “came together” refers to the beginning of their shared life, including sexual union.

verse.text: Joseph her husband, being righteous and not wanting to disgrace her publicly, decided to divorce her quietly.
verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English has two (righteous and just, righteousness and justice, justify), so the connection between these words is harder to see in English. Here the word describes a man who lives in accordance with God’s law. Whether Joseph’s reluctance to shame Mary is an expression of that righteousness or a mercy that tempers it is left open by the Greek.

verse.text: But when he had thought this over, look, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying, “Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary your wife into your home, for what has been conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit.

note.term: to take Mary your wife into your home
note.traditional: to take Mary as your wife

verse.note: The Greek calls Mary “your wife” already, since betrothal made her so in law. The verb means to take someone along or receive them to oneself, and here refers to the second stage of marriage, when the husband brought his bride into his house. The traditional wording suggests the marriage itself had yet to be contracted.

text.q: She will give birth to a son, and you are to call his name Jesus, for it is he who will save his people from their sins.”

verse.note: “Jesus” is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Joshua (Yeshua), which was understood to mean “the LORD saves”. The angel’s explanation, “for it is he who will save”, depends on that meaning. The wordplay is invisible in Greek as it is in English.

verse.text: All this happened so that what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet would be fulfilled:
“Look, the virgin will become pregnant and will give birth to a son, and they will call his name Emmanuel,” which is translated “God with us.”
verse.note: The quotation is Isaiah 7:14 in its Greek form. The Greek word normally means a virgin, while the Hebrew word in Isaiah means a young woman of marriageable age without specifying virginity. Matthew cites the verse as it stood in the Greek Scriptures his readers knew.

verse.text: When Joseph woke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him and took his wife into his home,
but he did not sleep with her until she had given birth to a son; and he called his name Jesus.
verse.note: The Greek says literally that he “was not knowing her”, a biblical idiom for sexual intercourse familiar from the Septuagint. A modern reader may not recognise the idiom, so an equivalent English euphemism is used. The Greek tense indicates continued abstention over the period.

The Greek construction states what was the case up to the birth and does not in itself say what happened afterwards. Traditions that hold Mary remained a virgin read it as silent about the later period; most Protestant interpreters take it to imply ordinary marital relations after the birth. The grammar alone does not settle the question.

verse.text: After Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of King Herod, look, magi from the east arrived in Jerusalem,
verse.note: This is Herod the Great, who ruled Judea as a client king under Rome and died in 4 BC. He was known for great building projects, including the rebuilding of the Jerusalem temple, and for ruthlessness toward anyone he saw as a rival, including members of his own family.

The Greek word originally named a Persian priestly class and by this period was used for eastern experts in astrology, dream interpretation and similar arts. “Wise men” is too general, and the text says nothing of their being kings or three in number. Several modern translations also use “Magi”. The same word can be used negatively of a sorcerer, as in Acts 13.

verse.text: saying, “Where is the one who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star at its rising and have come to pay him homage.”
verse.note: The Greek word means both “rising” (of a heavenly body) and “east”. In verse 1 “from the east” uses the plural without the article, the usual idiom for the direction. Here the singular with the article more naturally refers to the star’s rising, a technical astronomical expression. Most recent translations agree, though “in the east” remains possible.

The verb describes bowing or prostrating oneself before a superior, whether a king or a god. The magi are looking for a newborn king, and Herod uses the same word in verse 8, so royal homage is the sense on the characters’ lips. Many interpreters think Matthew intends his readers to see more in the act than the magi knew, and “worship” is the long-standing rendering.

verse.text: When King Herod heard this, he was alarmed, and all Jerusalem with him,
and gathering all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where the Messiah was to be born.
verse.note: Herod is asking about a title, the anointed king whom Israel expected, not using a name for Jesus. “Messiah” conveys that title to a modern reader, for whom “Christ” sounds like a proper name. Several modern translations make the same distinction, using “Messiah” where the title is under discussion and “Christ” elsewhere.

verse.text: They told him, “In Bethlehem of Judea, for so it is written through the prophet:

text.q: ‘And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the leaders of Judah; for out of you will come a leader who will shepherd my people Israel.’”

verse.note: The quotation is from Micah 5:2, with a final line that echoes 2 Samuel 5:2 on David as shepherd of Israel. Its wording differs from both the Hebrew and the Greek Old Testament, which describe Bethlehem as small among the clans of Judah. In Matthew’s form the town is no longer insignificant because of the ruler who comes from it.

verse.text: Then Herod secretly summoned the magi and carefully ascertained from them the time of the star’s appearing,
and he sent them to Bethlehem, saying, “Go and inquire carefully about the child, and when you have found him, report to me, so that I too may come and pay him homage.”
After hearing the king, they set out, and look, the star they had seen at its rising went ahead of them until it came and stood over the place where the child was.
When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy.
Entering the house, they saw the child with Mary his mother, and they fell down and paid him homage. Then, opening their treasure chests, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.
And having been warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they withdrew to their own country by another road.

After they had withdrawn, look, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying, “Get up, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt, and stay there until I tell you, for Herod is about to search for the child to destroy him.”
So he got up, took the child and his mother by night, and withdrew to Egypt,
and he was there until Herod’s death, so that what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled: “Out of Egypt I called my son.”

note.term: Out of Egypt I called my son

verse.note: The quotation is Hosea 11:1, where “my son” is the people of Israel brought out of Egypt in the exodus. Matthew presents Jesus as retracing Israel’s story. The wording follows the Hebrew text and not the Greek Old Testament, which reads “his children”.

verse.text: Then Herod, seeing that he had been made a fool of by the magi, was furious, and he sent and killed all the boys in Bethlehem and in all its surrounding district who were two years old and under, according to the time he had carefully ascertained from the magi.
verse.note: The Greek noun is in the masculine plural, and since Herod is hunting a male rival, most modern translations render it “boys” or “male children”. The older English tradition has “children”. A masculine plural can in principle cover both sexes, but the context favours the narrower sense.

verse.text: Then what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled:

text.q: “A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and loud lamentation: Rachel weeping for her children, and she refused to be comforted, because they are no more.”

verse.note: The quotation is Jeremiah 31:15, a lament over Israelites going into exile, with Ramah, a town north of Jerusalem, as its setting. Rachel, wife of Jacob, is pictured as the mother of the nation mourning her descendants. Genesis places her burial on the road to Bethlehem, which helps explain the link Matthew draws.

verse.text: After Herod died, look, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt,
saying, “Get up, take the child and his mother, and go to the land of Israel, for those who were seeking the child’s life have died.”
So he got up, took the child and his mother, and went into the land of Israel.
But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there. And having been warned in a dream, he withdrew to the region of Galilee,
verse.note: On Herod’s death his territory was divided among his sons. Archelaus received Judea, Samaria and Idumea with the lesser title of ethnarch, so “reigning” is used loosely. His rule was harsh enough that Rome removed him in AD 6. Galilee fell to his brother Herod Antipas.

verse.text: and he came and settled in a town called Nazareth, so that what was spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled, that he would be called a Nazarene.

note.term: that he would be called a Nazarene
note.traditional: He shall be called a Nazarene

verse.note: No Old Testament passage contains these words, and Matthew refers to “the prophets” in the plural, so this is rendered as a summary and not a direct quotation. The Greek allows either. What Matthew has in mind is disputed: common proposals are a wordplay on the Hebrew for “branch” in Isaiah 11:1, or on “nazirite” as in Judges 13:5. The Greek form is sometimes spelled “Nazorean” in English.

verse.text: In those days John the Baptist arrived, proclaiming in the wilderness of Judea
and saying, “Turn back, for the kingdom of the heavens has come near.”
verse.note: 'Repent' now suggests mainly feeling sorry. The Greek word, as used in the Gospels, carries the Hebrew prophets' call to 'return' to God: a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep 'repent' as an established term understood to include a change of life. The related noun in verses 8 and 11 is rendered 'turning back'.

The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase characteristic of Matthew, and the plural is kept here. Most translations flatten it to 'heaven'. The phrase is Matthew's usual equivalent of 'the kingdom of God' in the other Gospels.

The Greek perfect tense describes something that has drawn near and now stands close. Whether this means the kingdom is on the point of arriving or has in some sense already arrived is debated. The rendering leaves the question as open as the Greek does.

verse.text: For this is the one spoken of through Isaiah the prophet, who said: “A voice of one crying out in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.’”
verse.note: The quotation is Isaiah 40:3 in its Greek form. In Isaiah 'the Lord' is Israel's God, returning to his people through the desert. Matthew applies the passage to John as the one preparing the way for Jesus.

verse.text: Now John himself wore clothing of camel’s hair and a leather belt around his waist, and his food was locusts and wild honey.

note.term: a leather belt around his waist
note.traditional: a leather belt around his waist

verse.note: The description recalls the prophet Elijah, who is identified in 2 Kings 1:8 by his hairy garment and leather belt. A reader familiar with the Scriptures would have caught the allusion, and Matthew later connects John with Elijah explicitly.

verse.text: Then Jerusalem and all Judea and all the region around the Jordan were going out to him,
and they were being baptized by him in the Jordan River, confessing their sins.
But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them, “Brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?
verse.note: The Greek can mean that the Pharisees and Sadducees were coming to be baptized, or only that they were coming to the place where John was baptizing, perhaps to observe. John's question about fleeing the coming wrath favours the first, but the phrase does not settle it.

text.q: So produce fruit worthy of your turning back,
and do not presume to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that God is able to raise up children for Abraham from these stones.
Already the axe lies at the root of the trees; so every tree that does not produce good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.
I baptize you in water for turning back, but the one coming after me is stronger than I am; I am not fit to carry his sandals. He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire.

verse.note: The Greek preposition can mark either the element in which someone is immersed ('in') or the means used ('with'). Many translations have 'with water' and 'with the Holy Spirit'. Because the verb describes dipping or immersing, 'in' is used here for both phrases.

It is disputed whether 'fire' is a second image for the purifying work of the Spirit, or a separate baptism of judgment for those who do not turn back. The fire that destroys in verses 10 and 12 supports the second reading, but many interpreters hold that both purification and judgment are in view.

text.q: His winnowing shovel is in his hand, and he will clean out his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the storehouse, but the chaff he will burn up with unquenchable fire.”

verse.note: The Greek word names the shovel used to toss threshed grain into the wind, so that the light chaff blew away and the heavier grain fell back to the floor. Greek has a different word for the fork. Most modern translations say 'winnowing fork', and the picture is the same either way.

verse.text: Then Jesus arrived at the Jordan from Galilee, coming to John to be baptized by him.
But John tried to stop him, saying, “I need to be baptized by you, and you come to me?”
But Jesus answered him, “Allow it for now, for in this way it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” Then he allowed him.
verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice, and the verb 'justify', all share a single Greek root. The word covers being in the right, doing what God requires, and God's own action to set things right. Here most interpreters take 'fulfill all righteousness' to mean doing everything God's will requires, though exactly why Jesus' baptism belongs to that is debated.

verse.text: When Jesus had been baptized, he came up at once from the water. And look, the heavens were opened, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him.

note.traditional: the heavens were opened to him

verse.note: Many manuscripts add 'to him' after 'were opened', which would make the vision more clearly Jesus' own experience. Some of the earliest witnesses lack the words, and the Greek text followed here omits them.

verse.text: And look, a voice from the heavens, saying, “This is my Son, the beloved, in whom I delight.”

note.traditional: with whom I am well pleased

verse.note: The verb, in the Greek Old Testament, regularly expresses God's delight in or favour toward someone. 'Well pleased' can sound like mere approval, so 'delight' is used. The declaration echoes Psalm 2:7 ('You are my son') and Isaiah 42:1, where God speaks of his chosen servant in whom his soul delights.

verse.text: Then Jesus was led up into the wilderness by the Spirit to be tested by the devil.
verse.note: The Greek verb covers both testing someone's character and enticing them to do wrong; English has to choose. Most translations keep “tempted” here, since the devil's aim is to draw Jesus into sin. “Tested” is used because all three of Jesus' replies come from Deuteronomy 6–8, where Israel is tested in the wilderness for forty years, and because it keeps the link with “the tester” in verse 3 and “put to the test” in verse 7, which share the same Greek root.

verse.text: He fasted forty days and forty nights, and afterward he was hungry.
And the tester came up and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, tell these stones to become loaves of bread.”
But he answered, “It is written: ‘It is not on bread alone that a person will live, but on every word that comes out through the mouth of God.’”
Then the devil took him to the holy city and set him on the pinnacle of the temple,
verse.note: The Greek word means literally “little wing” and refers to some projecting or elevated part of the temple complex. Exactly which part is unknown; suggestions include a corner of the outer colonnade above the Kidron valley, a parapet, or the roof edge of the sanctuary. The traditional “pinnacle” is kept, but it should not be pictured as a spire.

verse.text: and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down, for it is written: ‘He will give his angels orders concerning you, and they will lift you up on their hands, so that you never strike your foot against a stone.’”
Jesus said to him, “Again, it is written: ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’”
Again the devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory,
and said to him, “All these I will give you, if you fall down and worship me.”
Then Jesus said to him, “Go away, Satan! For it is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.’”
verse.note: Many later manuscripts read “Get behind me, Satan,” matching Jesus' words to Peter in 16:23. The shorter reading is found in the earliest witnesses and is generally judged original, the longer one being an assimilation to the later passage.

verse.text: Then the devil left him, and look, angels came and waited on him.
When he heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee.
verse.note: Most translations say John was “arrested” or “put in prison,” which is what happened. The Greek verb means simply “handed over,” and Matthew goes on to use the same verb repeatedly for what will happen to Jesus. Keeping the literal sense lets the reader hear that parallel between John's fate and Jesus'.

verse.text: And leaving Nazareth, he went and settled in Capernaum by the sea, in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali,
so that what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled:

text.q: “Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles:

verse.note: The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples,” and in the plural it commonly refers to the non-Jewish peoples. This translation renders the one Greek word as “Gentiles” or “nations” according to context. The quotation is from Isaiah 9:1–2; Galilee lay on Israel's northern edge, bordered by non-Jewish populations.

text.q: the people sitting in darkness have seen a great light, and on those sitting in the land and shadow of death a light has dawned.”

verse.text: From then on Jesus began to proclaim and say, “Turn back, for the kingdom of the heavens has come near.”
verse.note: “Repent” in modern English centres on feeling sorry. The Greek word here carries the prophets' call to “return” to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep “repent” as an established term that readers understand to include a change of life.

Matthew's phrase is plural in Greek, “the kingdom of the heavens,” reflecting a Hebrew and Aramaic way of speaking. Most translations flatten it to “kingdom of heaven.” The plural is kept because a first-century hearer would have noticed this Semitic turn of phrase.

verse.text: As he was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon who is called Peter and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen.
And he said to them, “Come, follow me, and I will make you fishers of people.”
At once they left their nets and followed him.
Going on from there, he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets, and he called them.
At once they left the boat and their father and followed him.
And he went around the whole of Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, proclaiming the good news of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness among the people.
verse.note: The Greek word was an ordinary term for welcome news, especially a public announcement such as a victory or a ruler's accession. “Gospel” has become a religious technical term and a name for a kind of book, neither of which the first hearers would have heard here. Many modern translations also use “good news,” while others keep “gospel” for continuity.

verse.text: The report about him spread into the whole of Syria, and they brought to him all who were unwell, gripped by various diseases and torments, those possessed by demons, epileptics, and the paralyzed, and he healed them.
verse.note: The Greek word means literally “moonstruck,” reflecting the ancient belief that certain recurring afflictions were governed by the moon. The symptoms described under the same word in Matthew 17:15 resemble seizures, so most modern translations render it “epileptics.” The Greek does not make a medical diagnosis in the modern sense.

verse.text: And large crowds followed him from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and beyond the Jordan.
verse.note: The Decapolis (“Ten Cities”) was a group of largely Greek-speaking, predominantly non-Jewish cities, most of them east of the Jordan and the Sea of Galilee. Its mention suggests that Jesus' reputation reached beyond Jewish territory.

verse.text: When he saw the crowds, he went up the mountain, and after he had sat down his disciples came to him.
Then he opened his mouth and began to teach them, saying:

text.q: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of the heavens.

verse.note: The Greek is plural, following Hebrew and Aramaic idiom, in which the word for heaven is always plural. Most English versions flatten it to 'heaven'; this translation keeps the plural wherever the Greek has it and God's dwelling is meant. 'Kingdom of the heavens' is Matthew's characteristic expression for what the other Gospels call the kingdom of God.

text.q: Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.
Blessed are the gentle, for they will inherit the earth.

verse.note: 'Meek' now suggests weakness, which the Greek does not; 'gentle' or 'humble' is the mainstream modern rendering. The line echoes Psalm 37:11 (Septuagint 36:11), where the word renders the Hebrew for the humble poor and what they inherit is the land. The Greek word translated 'earth' here can mean either 'land' or 'earth'.

text.q: Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be satisfied.

verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two: 'righteous' and 'just', 'righteousness' and 'justice' all translate the same root. 'Righteousness' is the mainstream English rendering and is kept, though translations into most other languages use their word for justice and some scholars prefer it in English. In Matthew the word chiefly means conduct that is right in God's eyes; some take the hunger here to be for God to set things right.

text.q: Blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy.
Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God.
Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God.

note.traditional: children of God (KJV, NRSV, NIV); sons of God (ESV, NASB)

verse.note: The Greek says 'sons', and many versions render 'children' because women are plainly included. 'Sons' is kept here and in verse 45 because in Semitic idiom a 'son of' someone is one who shares that person's character, which is the point of both verses: those who make peace and love enemies resemble their Father.

text.q: Blessed are those who have been persecuted for the sake of righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of the heavens.
Blessed are you when people insult you and persecute you and falsely say every kind of evil against you on my account.
Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in the heavens; for that is how they persecuted the prophets who were before you.
“You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt loses its taste, what will make it salty again? It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled underfoot by people.
You are the light of the world. A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden.

note.traditional: a city set on a hill

verse.note: The Greek word is the same one translated 'mountain' in verse 1 and covers any height from a hill upward. English versions traditionally say 'hill' here. The rendering is kept uniform so the reader can see that it is one word.

text.q: Nor do people light a lamp and put it under a basket; they put it on the lampstand, and it gives light to everyone in the house.
In the same way, let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father in the heavens.
“Do not think that I came to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I did not come to abolish but to fulfill.
For truly I tell you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke of a letter will pass away from the Law until everything has taken place.

So whoever sets aside one of the least of these commandments and teaches people to do the same will be called least in the kingdom of the heavens; but whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of the heavens.
For I tell you that unless your righteousness goes far beyond that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of the heavens.
“You have heard that it was said to the people of long ago, ‘You shall not murder; and whoever murders will be liable to judgment.’

But I tell you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment; whoever says to his brother, ‘Raka,’ will be liable to the council; and whoever says, ‘Fool!’ will be liable to the Gehenna of fire.

note.traditional: angry with his brother without a cause

verse.note: Many later manuscripts add 'without cause' after 'brother', and the King James Version follows them. The earliest witnesses lack the word, and most editors judge it a scribal softening of an unqualified statement.

Matthew leaves this term of abuse untranslated; it is usually explained as Aramaic for 'empty one', roughly 'blockhead' or 'good-for-nothing'. The 'council' is the Sanhedrin, a judicial body. The three penalties rise steeply while the offences scarcely differ; whether the escalation is literal or deliberately ironic is disputed.

note.traditional: hell (hell fire; the hell of fire)

verse.note: Gehenna is a place name: the Valley of Hinnom beside Jerusalem, associated in the Hebrew Scriptures with child sacrifice and by the first century a name for the place of final fiery judgment. Many translations render it 'hell', usually with a footnote. The name is kept here because 'hell' merges it with Hades and with later imagery.

text.q: So if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you,
leave your gift there in front of the altar and first go and be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift.
Come to terms quickly with your accuser while you are with him on the way, or your accuser may hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the officer, and you will be thrown into prison.
Truly I tell you, you will never get out of there until you have paid back the last penny.
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’
But I tell you that everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.

note.traditional: looks at a woman lustfully; looks on a woman to lust after her

verse.note: The Greek construction normally expresses purpose: looking with the aim of desiring. The verb is the one the Septuagint uses in the commandment 'You shall not covet your neighbor's wife', and the word for 'woman' also means 'wife', so some read 'looks at another man's wife in order to covet her'. The traditional 'lustfully' is not wrong but hides the echo of the commandment.

text.q: If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you; for it is better for you that one part of your body be lost than that your whole body be thrown into Gehenna.
And if your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you; for it is better for you that one part of your body be lost than that your whole body go off into Gehenna.
“It was also said, ‘Whoever divorces his wife must give her a certificate of divorce.’
But I tell you that everyone who divorces his wife, except on the ground of sexual immorality, makes her commit adultery, and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.

verse.note: The Greek word is a broad term for unlawful sexual activity. Here it is most often taken to mean adultery or other sexual infidelity by the wife; others have argued for premarital unchastity discovered after the wedding, or for marriages within forbidden degrees of kinship. The exception clause appears only in Matthew (here and 19:9), and its scope remains disputed.

text.q: “Again, you have heard that it was said to the people of long ago, ‘You shall not swear falsely, but shall keep your oaths to the Lord.’
But I tell you not to swear at all: neither by heaven, for it is God’s throne;
nor by the earth, for it is the footstool of his feet; nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King;
nor shall you swear by your head, for you cannot make a single hair white or black.
Let your word be ‘Yes, yes’ or ‘No, no’; anything beyond these is from the evil one.
“You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’
But I tell you not to resist the evil person. Instead, whoever slaps you on the right cheek, turn the other to him as well;

note.traditional: resist not evil; do not resist an evil person

verse.note: The Greek form can be masculine ('the evil person') or neuter ('evil' in the abstract); the examples that follow, all about individuals who wrong you, favour the personal sense. The same form in verse 37 is taken as 'the evil one', the devil, though 'from evil' is possible there. The verb 'resist' can also mean to oppose in court or to retaliate with force, and some take the command in that narrower sense.

text.q: and if anyone wants to sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well;
and whoever forces you into service for one mile, go with him two.

note.traditional: compel thee to go a mile; forces you to go one mile

verse.note: The verb is a technical term for compulsory requisition of labour or transport by officials or soldiers. It is the word used when Simon of Cyrene is made to carry the cross (27:32). A hearer in Roman-ruled territory would think of a soldier commandeering a passer-by to carry his pack.

text.q: Give to the one who asks you, and do not turn away from the one who wants to borrow from you.
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’

verse.note: 'Love your neighbor' is Leviticus 19:18. 'Hate your enemy' is not found in the Jewish Scriptures; it appears to summarise a popular inference or a teaching current in some circles. Comparable language about hating the 'sons of darkness' occurs in the Community Rule among the Dead Sea Scrolls.

text.q: But I tell you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you,

note.term: love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you
note.traditional: love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you

verse.note: Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, have a longer form of this verse. The extra clauses are generally judged to have been imported from the parallel in Luke 6:27–28; the earliest witnesses have the short form translated here.

text.q: so that you may become sons of your Father in the heavens; for he makes his sun rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous.
For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same?
And if you greet only your brothers, what more are you doing than anyone else? Do not even the Gentiles do the same?
So you shall be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.

verse.note: The Greek word means complete, whole or mature, having reached its goal, rather than flawless. In context it points to a love that is whole and undivided, extended to enemies as well as friends, as the Father's is; the Septuagint uses the word for wholehearted devotion to God (Deuteronomy 18:13). 'Perfect' is kept as the traditional rendering, but 'complete' or 'whole' is defensible.

text.q: Take care not to practice your righteousness in front of people in order to be seen by them; otherwise you have no reward with your Father who is in the heavens.

verse.note: Here the word means doing what is right in practice. It heads the three examples that follow: giving to the needy, prayer and fasting. Greek has a single word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice), so the same word can elsewhere be rendered 'justice'.

The Greek is plural here and in verse 9, a Semitic turn of phrase that Matthew uses often for God's dwelling. Most translations flatten it to 'heaven'. This translation keeps the plural where the Greek has it and the singular where the Greek is singular, as in verses 10 and 20.

text.q: So when you give to the needy, do not sound a trumpet ahead of you, as the performers do in the synagogues and in the streets, so that people will praise them. Truly I tell you, they have been paid their reward in full.

verse.note: The Greek word originally meant a stage actor, but in Jewish Greek before the New Testament it already meant a godless or insincere person, and elsewhere this translation renders it 'hypocrites'. In this chapter the passage is about religion staged for an audience, with trumpets, street corners and being seen. The theatrical sense is therefore live, and 'performers' is used in verses 2, 5 and 16.

note.term: they have been paid their reward in full

verse.note: The verb is the standard term on surviving receipts from the period for acknowledging payment in full, so hearers would have caught a commercial tone. The account is settled and nothing further is owed. Many modern translations similarly render 'they have received their reward in full'.

text.q: But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing,
so that your giving may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.

And when you pray, you are not to be like the performers; for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and on the corners of the main streets, so that people will see them. Truly I tell you, they have been paid their reward in full.
But you, when you pray, go into your inner room, shut your door, and pray to your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.
And when you pray, do not babble on like the Gentiles, for they think they will be heard because of their many words.

verse.note: The Greek verb is extremely rare and its exact sense is uncertain. Its meaning is inferred mainly from the parallel 'many words' later in the verse. Proposals include babbling, stammering and repeating empty phrases.

text.q: So do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him.
You, then, are to pray like this: ‘Our Father in the heavens, may your name be held holy,

note.term: may your name be held holy

verse.note: 'Hallowed' is the traditional word but is now archaic. The Greek is a request that God's name be treated as holy, matching the two requests that follow. It may ask that people honor the name, that God act to vindicate it, or both. The Greek passive leaves that open.

text.q: may your kingdom come, may your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth.
Give us today our daily bread,

verse.note: This Greek word is almost unknown outside the Lord's Prayer, and its meaning is uncertain. The main proposals are 'for the coming day', 'necessary for existence' and 'for today'. With no secure alternative, the traditional 'daily' is kept.

text.q: and forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors;
and do not bring us into testing, but rescue us from the evil one.’

verse.note: The Greek word covers both a trial that tests a person and an enticement to sin, whereas English 'temptation' now suggests only the second. Many scholars take the petition as asking to be spared a time of trial, and some think specifically of the final ordeal before the end. The traditional sense remains possible.

The Greek form can be masculine ('the evil one', meaning the devil) or neuter ('evil' in general), and the grammar does not settle it. Matthew clearly uses the expression for the devil elsewhere, which favors the personal reading, but both are widely held.

note.term: rescue us from the evil one
note.traditional: For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever. Amen.

verse.note: The familiar closing doxology is absent from the earliest manuscripts and is not part of the SBLGNT text translated here. It appears in later manuscripts in varying forms. It is generally thought to have entered the text from the prayer's early use in worship.

text.q: For if you forgive people their offenses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you;
but if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive your offenses.
And when you fast, do not look gloomy like the performers, for they make their faces unsightly so that people will see them fasting. Truly I tell you, they have been paid their reward in full.
But you, when you fast, put oil on your head and wash your face,
so that your fasting will be seen not by people but by your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.
Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break in and steal;
but store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys, and where thieves do not break in or steal.
For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
The lamp of the body is the eye. So if your eye is generous, your whole body will be full of light;

verse.note: The Greek word means 'single' or 'sound', and most translations keep the physical image with 'healthy'. The saying sits between treasure in heaven and slavery to wealth, however, and the contrasting 'evil eye' was a Jewish idiom for stinginess. The saying is therefore taken to be about generosity. The physical picture of a sound eye is lost in this rendering.

text.q: but if your eye is stingy, your whole body will be full of darkness. So if the light within you is darkness, how great that darkness is!

verse.note: Literally 'if your eye is evil'. In Jewish usage an 'evil eye' meant a grudging, miserly attitude toward others, as in Matthew 20:15, not the casting of a curse. Translations that keep the physical image render 'bad' or 'unhealthy'.

text.q: No one can be a slave to two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot be a slave to both God and wealth.

verse.note: The verb is the ordinary word for a slave's service to an owner, and 'masters' here are slave-owners. The point is that a slave belongs wholly to one master. 'Serve' in modern English suggests employment, which can be shared between employers.

The Greek text keeps an Aramaic word, mamona, meaning wealth or property, which older English versions carried over as 'mammon'. In sources of the period it is an ordinary word and not the name of a god or demon. The personification comes from setting it beside God as a rival master.

text.q: For this reason I tell you: do not worry about your life, what you will eat, or about your body, what you will wear. Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing?
Look at the birds of the sky: they do not sow or reap or gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth much more than they are?
And which of you by worrying can add a single hour to your span of life?

note.term: a single hour to your span of life
note.traditional: add one cubit unto his stature

verse.note: The Greek says literally 'add one cubit', a measure of length of about half a metre. The noun that follows can mean either age or bodily height. Most modern translations take it as a measure of length applied figuratively to lifespan, since adding a cubit to one's height would be no small thing. The older rendering takes it of stature.

text.q: And why do you worry about clothing? Consider how the lilies of the field grow: they do not labor or spin.
Yet I tell you that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these.
But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, you of little faith?
So do not worry, saying, ‘What are we to eat?’ or ‘What are we to drink?’ or ‘What are we to wear?’
For it is the Gentiles who seek after all these things; and your heavenly Father knows that you need them all.
But seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.

verse.note: Many manuscripts read 'the kingdom of God and his righteousness'. The SBLGNT follows the shorter reading, literally 'the kingdom and his righteousness', where 'his' refers to the heavenly Father of verse 32. The pronoun is taken here with both nouns.

text.q: So do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself. Each day has enough trouble of its own.
Do not judge, so that you will not be judged.
For by the judgment you judge with, you will be judged, and by the measure you measure with, it will be measured to you.
Why do you look at the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not notice the beam in your own eye?

verse.note: The word means a heavy structural timber such as a roof beam, while the 'speck' is a tiny bit of chaff, straw or wood. The contrast is deliberately absurd: someone with a rafter in his eye offers to remove a splinter from another's.

text.q: Or how can you say to your brother, ‘Let me take the speck out of your eye,’ and look, the beam is in your own eye?
Hypocrite! First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother’s eye.
Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls in front of pigs, or they may trample them under their feet and turn and tear you apart.

verse.note: Dogs in this setting were scavengers rather than pets, and pigs were unclean animals; both were stock images of what is unfit for sacred things. 'What is holy' may call to mind consecrated food from the temple offerings, which was not to be given to animals. Many interpreters read the saying as a crossed pattern, with the pigs trampling and the dogs turning to attack. Whom the saying has in view is disputed.

text.q: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.
For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.
Or is there anyone among you who, when his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone?
Or when he asks for a fish, will give him a snake?
So if you, evil as you are, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in the heavens give good things to those who ask him!

verse.note: The Greek is plural here and in verse 21 ('kingdom of the heavens', 'Father in the heavens'), reflecting a Semitic way of speaking that a first-century hearer would have recognized. Most English translations flatten it to the singular 'heaven'. The plural is kept here because the Greek has it.

text.q: So whatever you want people to do for you, do just that for them as well; for this is the Law and the Prophets.

verse.note: 'The Law and the Prophets' was a common way of referring to the Jewish Scriptures as a whole by their two main divisions. Jesus presents this rule as a summary of what they require. A negative form of the saying, not doing to others what you would hate, was already known in Jewish tradition, for example in Tobit 4:15.

text.q: Enter through the narrow gate. For wide is the gate and spacious the road that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter through it.
For narrow is the gate and constricted the road that leads to life, and few are those who find it.

verse.note: Manuscripts divide here between a word meaning 'for' or 'because' and one giving an exclamation, 'How narrow is the gate!' The SBLGNT prints the first, which is translated here. Many manuscripts and several modern editions have the exclamation. The sense of the passage is little affected.

The participle means 'pressed' or 'squeezed'. It can describe a road that is physically tight, the natural opposite of the 'spacious' road in verse 13, and that is the reading taken here. The same verb is the ordinary word for being afflicted or oppressed, so some translations render 'the way is hard', and a hearer may well have caught both senses.

text.q: Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inside are rapacious wolves.
By their fruits you will recognize them. People do not gather grapes from thornbushes, or figs from thistles, do they?
In the same way, every good tree produces fine fruit, but the rotten tree produces bad fruit.
A good tree cannot produce bad fruit, nor can a rotten tree produce fine fruit.
Every tree that does not produce fine fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.
So then, by their fruits you will recognize them.
Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of the heavens, but the one who does the will of my Father in the heavens.
Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name drive out demons, and in your name do many mighty works?’

verse.note: 'That day' is shorthand, drawn from the prophets, for the day of God's final judgment. Jesus here casts himself as the one before whom people plead on that day and who gives the verdict.

text.q: And then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you. Go away from me, you who practice lawlessness.’

note.traditional: ye that work iniquity / you workers of lawlessness

verse.note: The dismissal echoes Psalm 6:8 in its Greek form, 'Depart from me, all you who work lawlessness.' The Greek noun means disregard for God's law, which is sharper than the older English 'iniquity'. The charge is pointed, since those addressed claim impressive religious achievements in Jesus' name.

text.q: So everyone who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a sensible man who built his house on the rock.

verse.note: Most translations have 'wise'. The Greek word is not the usual term for wisdom (sophos). It describes practical good sense, the prudence of someone who thinks ahead and acts accordingly. 'Sensible' keeps that distinction and suits a builder who chooses his site with the storm in mind.

text.q: The rain came down, the torrents came, the winds blew and fell upon that house, yet it did not fall, for its foundation had been laid on the rock.
And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand.
The rain came down, the torrents came, the winds blew and struck against that house, and it fell, and great was its fall.”

verse.text: And when Jesus had finished these words, the crowds were astounded at his teaching,

note.term: when Jesus had finished these words
note.traditional: when Jesus had ended these sayings

verse.note: This formula, more literally 'and it happened, when Jesus finished these words', closes each of the five great blocks of teaching in Matthew (here and at 11:1, 13:53, 19:1 and 26:1). It marks the end of the discourse that began at 5:1, traditionally called the Sermon on the Mount.

verse.text: for he was teaching them as one who has authority, and not as their scribes.
verse.note: In the Jewish setting of the Gospels, scribes were not copyists but trained experts in the Law of Moses, who taught and interpreted it. The contrast is usually understood this way: they taught by appeal to Scripture and to received interpretation, whereas Jesus speaks on his own authority ('but I say to you').

verse.text: When he came down from the mountain, large crowds followed him.
And look, a man with a skin disease came up and bowed down before him, saying, “Lord, if you are willing, you can make me clean.”

note.term: a man with a skin disease

verse.note: The traditional 'leper' suggests Hansen's disease, which is what 'leprosy' means today. The Greek word, as used in the Septuagint for the condition regulated in Leviticus 13–14, covers a range of scaly skin conditions that made a person ritually unclean, which is why the man asks to be made 'clean' rather than healed. Most scholars agree the term is broader than modern leprosy, though many translations keep the familiar word.

The verb describes the physical act of prostrating oneself before a superior, whether a king, a patron or a god. Older translations render it 'worshipped'; many modern ones have 'knelt before him'. Whether Matthew means readers to see more than deep respect in the gesture here is debated, and the rendering leaves that open.

verse.text: He stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, “I am willing; be made clean.” And immediately his skin disease was cleansed.
And Jesus said to him, “See that you tell no one. But go, show yourself to the priest and offer the gift that Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.”
verse.note: Leviticus 14 required a person recovered from such a skin disease to be examined by a priest and to make an offering before returning to ordinary community life. 'Them' may be the priests or the people generally. The phrase could also be taken in a hostile sense, 'as evidence against them', but most interpreters read it as positive proof of the cure.

verse.text: When he entered Capernaum, a centurion came to him, pleading with him
and saying, “Lord, my servant is lying at home paralyzed, terribly tormented.”
verse.note: The Greek word can mean either a child ('my boy', 'my son') or a servant of any age. Most translations choose 'servant', partly because Luke's parallel account calls him a slave; a minority of scholars argue for 'son'. It is a different word from the one rendered 'slave' in verse 9.

verse.text: He said to him, “I will come and heal him.”

note.term: I will come and heal him

verse.note: The Greek can equally be read as a question, with an emphatic 'I': 'Am I to come and heal him?' On that reading Jesus hesitates over entering a Gentile's house, and the centurion's reply in verse 8 answers the hesitation. Most translations take it as a statement, but a number of scholars prefer the question.

verse.text: The centurion answered, “Lord, I am not worthy for you to come under my roof. But only say the word, and my servant will be healed.

text.q: For I too am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my slave, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.”

verse.note: The word denotes a person owned by another, not a hired employee, and a first-century reader would have understood it so. Many English versions soften it to 'servant'. 'Slave' also keeps it distinct from the different word translated 'servant' in verses 6, 8 and 13.

verse.text: When Jesus heard this, he was amazed and said to those who were following, “Truly I tell you, with no one in Israel have I found such faith.

note.term: with no one in Israel have I found such faith
note.traditional: I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel

verse.note: Many manuscripts read 'not even in Israel have I found such faith', which matches the wording of Luke 7:9. The reading translated here has early manuscript support, and editors generally judge that copyists were more likely to bring Matthew into line with Luke than the reverse.

text.q: I tell you that many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of the heavens,

verse.note: The Greek is plural, reflecting a Hebrew and Aramaic way of speaking that a first-century hearer would have noticed. Most translations flatten it to 'heaven'. The picture of reclining at table is of a banquet, where guests lay on couches to eat.

text.q: but the sons of the kingdom will be driven out into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

verse.note: 'Son of' something is a Semitic idiom for one who belongs to it or is its natural heir. Here it refers to those who would be expected to inherit the kingdom by birth, in contrast to the many who come from east and west.

verse.text: And Jesus said to the centurion, “Go; let it be done for you as you have believed.” And the servant was healed in that very hour.
When Jesus came into Peter’s house, he saw Peter’s mother-in-law lying there with a fever.
He touched her hand, and the fever left her, and she got up and began to serve him.
When evening came, they brought to him many who were demon-possessed, and he drove out the spirits with a word and healed all who were sick.
This was to fulfill what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet: “He himself took our sicknesses and carried our diseases.”

note.term: He himself took our sicknesses and carried our diseases

verse.note: The quotation is Isaiah 53:4. Matthew's wording stays close to the Hebrew, which speaks of sicknesses and pains, rather than the Septuagint, which speaks of sins. He applies the line to physical healing.

verse.text: Now when Jesus saw large crowds around him, he gave orders to cross to the other side.
And a scribe came up and said to him, “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go.”
Jesus said to him, “Foxes have dens and the birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.”
Another, one of the disciples, said to him, “Lord, allow me first to go and bury my father.”
But Jesus said to him, “Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead.”

note.term: leave the dead to bury their own dead

verse.note: Burying a parent was among the most serious family obligations in Jewish life, which is what makes the saying so startling. Some interpreters think the father had not yet died and the man was asking to stay at home until he did, but the Greek does not say so. The first 'dead' is usually understood figuratively, of those who do not respond to Jesus' call.

verse.text: When he got into the boat, his disciples followed him.
And look, a great storm shook the sea, so that the boat was being covered by the waves; but he was asleep.

note.term: a great storm shook the sea
note.traditional: there arose a great tempest in the sea

verse.note: The Greek noun means a shaking and is the usual word for an earthquake, as elsewhere in Matthew. Mark and Luke use an ordinary word for a squall in their accounts. 'Storm' is clearly what is meant, since waves and winds follow, and the verb 'shook' is supplied to keep the force of the unusual word.

verse.text: They came and woke him, saying, “Lord, save us! We are perishing!”
He said to them, “Why are you so afraid, you of little faith?” Then he got up and rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm.
The men were amazed and said, “What kind of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?”
When he came to the other side, to the region of the Gadarenes, two demon-possessed men met him, coming out from the tombs. They were so fierce that no one could pass along that road.
verse.note: Manuscripts vary between Gadarenes, Gerasenes and Gergesenes, here and in the parallel passages in Mark and Luke. Gadara and Gerasa were both cities of the Decapolis, Gadara several miles from the lake and Gerasa much farther. Most editors judge 'Gadarenes' to be the original reading in Matthew.

verse.text: And look, they cried out, “What have you to do with us, Son of God? Have you come here before the appointed time to torment us?”
Now some distance away from them a large herd of pigs was feeding.
The demons pleaded with him, “If you drive us out, send us into the herd of pigs.”
He said to them, “Go!” So they came out and went off into the pigs; and look, the whole herd rushed down the steep bank into the sea and died in the waters.
Those tending them fled, and going off into the town they reported everything, including what had happened to the demon-possessed men.
And look, the whole town came out to meet Jesus, and when they saw him they pleaded with him to move on from their region.
Getting into a boat, he crossed over and came to his own town.
verse.note: This is Capernaum, on the Sea of Galilee, where Matthew has said Jesus settled after leaving Nazareth (4:13). The Greek word covers any settlement larger than a village; “town” fits a place of Capernaum’s size better than “city.”

verse.text: Some people brought him a paralyzed man lying on a bed. Seeing their faith, Jesus said to the paralyzed man, “Take heart, child; your sins are forgiven.”
verse.note: The Greek word is the general term for a child of either sex, used here as an affectionate address. Most English versions have “son” because the person addressed is a man, but Greek has a separate word for “son,” and Matthew did not use it.

verse.text: At this some of the scribes said to themselves, “This man is blaspheming.”
Knowing their thoughts, Jesus said, “Why are you thinking evil things in your hearts?

text.q: For which is easier: to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Get up and walk’?

verse.text: But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins—” then he said to the paralyzed man, “Get up, pick up your bed, and go to your home.”
And he got up and went off to his home.
When the crowds saw this, they were afraid, and they glorified God, who had given such authority to human beings.
As Jesus went on from there, he saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, “Follow me.” And he got up and followed him.
verse.note: This was a station where tolls and customs duties were collected on goods in transit. The collectors worked under contract for the ruling power and were widely suspected of overcharging. Observant Jews therefore classed them with “sinners,” as in verses 10–11.

verse.text: And as he was reclining at table in the house, many tax collectors and sinners came and reclined with Jesus and his disciples.
verse.note: The Greek does not say whose house this is. The parallel in Luke 5:29 makes it the tax collector’s own house, and most readers assume the same here, but Matthew’s wording could also mean the house where Jesus was living in Capernaum. Diners at a formal meal reclined on couches, hence “reclining at table.”

verse.text: When the Pharisees saw this, they said to his disciples, “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?”
But when he heard this, he said, “Those who are well have no need of a doctor, but those who are sick do.

text.q: Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice.’ For I did not come to call the righteous but sinners.”

note.term: I desire mercy and not sacrifice
note.traditional: I desire mercy, and not sacrifice

verse.note: The quotation is Hosea 6:6, which Jesus cites again at 12:7. “Go and learn” is a teacher’s formula for sending a student back to study a text. The Hebrew word behind “mercy” means loyal, steadfast love, and the Septuagint regularly rendered it with the Greek word used here.

verse.text: Then the disciples of John came to him and asked, “Why do we and the Pharisees fast often, but your disciples do not fast?”
Jesus said to them, “Can the wedding guests mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? But days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast.

note.traditional: children of the bridechamber; wedding guests

verse.note: The Greek has a Semitic idiom, literally “sons of the wedding hall,” meaning those who belong to the wedding party. Some take it more narrowly as the bridegroom’s attendants. A wedding was a time of feasting, and fasting was a sign of mourning.

text.q: No one puts a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old cloak, for the patch pulls away from the cloak, and a worse tear results.
Nor do people put new wine into old wineskins. If they do, the skins burst, the wine spills out, and the skins are ruined. Instead they put new wine into fresh wineskins, and both are preserved.”

verse.text: While he was saying these things to them, an official came and bowed down before him, saying, “My daughter has just died. But come and lay your hand on her, and she will live.”
verse.note: The Greek word covers anyone holding a position of authority, from a king to a local magistrate or community leader. “Ruler” suggests a sovereign to a modern reader, which is not meant. Mark 5:22 and Luke 8:41 identify the man as a synagogue leader named Jairus. The same word is rendered “ruler” in verse 34, where the head of the demons is meant.

The verb describes the physical act of prostrating oneself or kneeling before a superior, whether a god, a king, or someone from whom a favour is begged. Older versions have “worshipped,” and Matthew may intend his readers to see more in the gesture than the official did. In the scene itself it is the posture of an urgent petitioner, and many modern versions render it “knelt before him.”

verse.text: Jesus got up and followed him, and so did his disciples.
Then a woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years came up behind him and touched the tassel of his cloak,
verse.note: The word can mean the edge of a garment, but it is also the Septuagint’s term for the tassels that Numbers 15:38–39 commands Israelites to wear on the corners of their garments. Matthew uses it in that sense at 23:5. Most scholars think the tassel is meant here, though “edge” remains possible.

verse.text: for she was saying to herself, “If I only touch his cloak, I will be made well.”
verse.note: The verb in verses 21–22 is the ordinary Greek word for “save” or “rescue,” used of deliverance from illness and danger as well as from sin. A Greek reader would hear both senses in “your faith has made you well.” English cannot keep both in one word, and the context here is healing.

verse.text: Jesus turned, saw her, and said, “Take heart, daughter; your faith has made you well.” And the woman was made well from that hour.
When Jesus came to the official’s house and saw the flute players and the crowd in an uproar,
verse.note: Pipers and wailing mourners were hired for funerals, which took place within hours of death. Their presence shows that the household regarded the girl as dead and that burial preparations had begun.

verse.text: he said, “Go away, for the girl has not died but is sleeping.” And they laughed at him.
But when the crowd had been put outside, he went in and took her by the hand, and the girl got up.
And the report of this went out through that whole region.
As Jesus went on from there, two blind men followed him, crying out, “Have mercy on us, Son of David!”
When he had gone into the house, the blind men came to him, and Jesus said to them, “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” They said to him, “Yes, Lord.”
Then he touched their eyes, saying, “Let it be done for you according to your faith.”
And their eyes were opened. Jesus sternly warned them, “See that no one knows of this.”
But they went out and spread the news about him through that whole region.
As they were going out, people brought to him a mute man possessed by a demon.
When the demon had been driven out, the mute man spoke. The crowds were amazed and said, “Nothing like this has ever been seen in Israel.”
But the Pharisees said, “By the ruler of the demons he drives out the demons.”

note.term: By the ruler of the demons he drives out the demons.
note.traditional: He casteth out devils through the prince of the devils

verse.note: A few early witnesses, chiefly of the so-called Western text, lack this verse, and some scholars think it was added from 12:24. The great majority of manuscripts include it, and the SBLGNT prints it without brackets.

verse.text: Jesus went around all the towns and villages, teaching in their synagogues, proclaiming the good news of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness.
When he saw the crowds, he was moved with compassion for them, because they were harassed and cast down, like sheep without a shepherd.
Then he said to his disciples, “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few.

text.q: So ask the Lord of the harvest to send out workers into his harvest.”

verse.note: The verb is the same one used in verses 33–34 for driving out demons and in verse 25 for putting the crowd outside. In this period it could also mean simply “send out” or “bring out” with no idea of force, which is the sense here, though it is a stronger word than the usual verb for sending.

verse.text: And calling his twelve disciples to him, he gave them authority over unclean spirits, to drive them out, and to heal every disease and every sickness.
The names of the twelve apostles are these: first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother; James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother;
Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus;
Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, who also handed him over.
verse.note: The Greek word transliterates an Aramaic term meaning 'zealous one'; it has nothing to do with Canaan or Cana. Luke's lists of the Twelve give the Greek equivalent, 'Simon the Zealot'. Whether the label marks Simon as a member of a revolutionary movement or simply as a man known for religious zeal is disputed.

The verb is the ordinary Greek word for handing a person over to an authority, and it is the same verb Jesus uses of the disciples' own fate in verses 17, 19 and 21. Most translations use 'betrayed' when Judas is the subject, which hides that link. The word itself does not say 'treachery', though the act it describes here was one.

verse.text: These twelve Jesus sent out with these instructions: “Do not go off on a road to the Gentiles, and do not enter a town of the Samaritans;
verse.note: Greek has a single word that means 'peoples' or 'nations' and, in Jewish usage in the plural, the non-Jewish peoples. This translation renders it 'Gentiles' or 'nations' according to sense, as most translations do. Here and in verse 18 the non-Jewish peoples are meant.

text.q: but go instead to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.
As you go, proclaim, ‘The kingdom of the heavens has come near.’

verse.note: Matthew's Greek is plural, here and in 'my Father in the heavens' (verses 32–33), reflecting a Hebrew and Aramaic way of speaking. Most English translations flatten the plural to 'heaven'. The plural is kept because a first-century hearer would have noticed it.

text.q: Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse those with skin disease, drive out demons. You received as a gift; give as a gift.

verse.note: The Greek word, like the Hebrew term it translates in the Septuagint, covers a range of scaly skin conditions that made a person ritually unclean; this is why the verb is 'cleanse' rather than 'heal'. It is not limited to, and may not include, the illness now called leprosy (Hansen's disease). Most translations keep 'lepers', often with a footnote saying the same.

text.q: Do not acquire gold or silver or copper for your belts,
or a bag for the road, or two tunics, or sandals, or a staff; for the worker is worthy of his food.
Whatever town or village you enter, find out who in it is worthy, and stay there until you leave.
As you enter the house, greet it;

verse.note: The customary Jewish greeting on entering a home was a wish of peace ('Peace to this house'). That is why the next verse can speak of 'your peace' coming upon the house or returning to the speaker: the greeting is treated as a real blessing given or withdrawn.

text.q: and if the house is worthy, let your peace come upon it; but if it is not worthy, let your peace return to you.
And if anyone does not welcome you or listen to your words, shake the dust off your feet as you leave that house or town.
Truly I tell you, it will be more bearable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that town.
Look, I am sending you out like sheep among wolves; so be as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves.
Be on your guard against people; for they will hand you over to councils and flog you in their synagogues,
and you will be brought before governors and kings for my sake, as a testimony to them and to the Gentiles.
But when they hand you over, do not worry about how you are to speak or what you are to say; for what you are to say will be given to you in that hour.
For it is not you who are speaking, but the Spirit of your Father speaking in you.
Brother will hand over brother to death, and a father his child; children will rise up against parents and have them put to death.
You will be hated by everyone because of my name; but the one who endures to the end will be saved.
When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next; for truly I tell you, you will certainly not finish going through the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes.

note.term: before the Son of Man comes
note.traditional: till the Son of man be come

verse.note: The wording echoes Daniel 7:13, where one 'like a son of man' comes with the clouds of heaven. What 'coming' is meant here is one of the most disputed questions in the Gospel: proposals include Jesus' resurrection and exaltation, the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, and his final return. The Greek does not settle the question.

text.q: A disciple is not above the teacher, nor a slave above his master.

verse.note: The Greek word means a person owned by a master, not a hired employee, and the saying depends on that relationship. Older English translations used 'servant'; several recent ones use 'slave'. The word translated 'master' is the same word elsewhere rendered 'lord'.

text.q: It is enough for the disciple to become like his teacher, and the slave like his master. If they called the master of the house Beelzebul, how much more the members of his household!

verse.note: A name for the ruler of the demons (see Matthew 12:24), which Jesus' opponents applied to him. Its origin is uncertain; it is probably related to a title of the Canaanite god Baal, and some think it could be heard as 'lord of the dwelling', which would give added point to 'master of the house'. The spelling 'Beelzebub' in older English Bibles comes from the Latin tradition, influenced by 2 Kings 1:2.

text.q: So do not be afraid of them; for there is nothing covered that will not be uncovered, and nothing hidden that will not be made known.
What I tell you in the dark, say in the light; and what you hear in your ear, proclaim on the housetops.
And do not be afraid of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; be afraid rather of the one who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.

verse.note: Gehenna is a place name: the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, which by Jesus' time had become the standard Jewish image for the place of final judgment. Many translations render it 'hell', usually with a footnote giving the name. The name is kept because 'hell' merges it with Hades, a different word, and with much later imagery.

text.q: Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? Yet not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father.
As for you, even the hairs of your head are all counted.
So do not be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows.
So everyone who acknowledges me before people, I too will acknowledge before my Father in the heavens;
but whoever denies me before people, I too will deny before my Father in the heavens.
Do not think that I came to bring peace to the earth; I did not come to bring peace but a sword.
For I came to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law;
and a person’s enemies will be the members of their own household.
Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me;
and whoever does not take up their cross and follow after me is not worthy of me.
Whoever finds their life will lose it, and whoever loses their life for my sake will find it.

verse.note: The Greek word is the same one rendered 'soul' in verse 28. It covers a person's life, self and inner being, and English has no single word for that range. 'Soul' is used in verse 28, where it is set against the body, and 'life' here, where the contrast is between saving and losing oneself; the reader should hear the two verses together.

text.q: Whoever welcomes you welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me.
Whoever welcomes a prophet because he is a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward, and whoever welcomes a righteous person because he is righteous will receive a righteous person’s reward.

note.traditional: in the name of a prophet

verse.note: The Greek says literally 'into the name of a prophet', a Semitic idiom meaning 'on the ground that he is a prophet'. The traditional literal rendering is obscure in English, and most modern translations paraphrase it in a similar way. The same idiom lies behind 'because he is righteous' here and 'because he is a disciple' in verse 42.

text.q: And whoever gives one of these little ones even a cup of cold water because he is a disciple—truly I tell you, that person will certainly not lose their reward.”

verse.text: When Jesus had finished giving instructions to his twelve disciples, he moved on from there to teach and proclaim in their towns.
Now when John heard in prison about the deeds of the Messiah, he sent word through his disciples
verse.note: Here the word has the article and works as a title for the anointed king Israel was expecting; John's question in the next verse is whether Jesus is that figure. 'Messiah' conveys the title to a modern reader, where 'Christ' tends to be heard as a name. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels.

verse.text: and asked him, “Are you the one who is coming, or are we to expect someone else?”
Jesus answered them, “Go and report to John what you hear and see:

text.q: the blind see again and the lame walk, lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, the dead are raised and the poor have good news announced to them.

verse.note: Jesus answers by listing what is happening, in language drawn from Isaiah's pictures of God's coming restoration (Isaiah 35:5–6; 61:1; compare 26:19). A hearer who knew those passages would take the list as an indirect yes to John's question.
