The Greek word covers a range of skin conditions, not only the disease now called leprosy. Under the law of Moses such conditions made a person ritually unclean and cut them off from ordinary community life, which is why the text speaks of being 'cleansed' and not simply healed.

text.q: And blessed is anyone who does not stumble because of me.”

note.traditional: is not offended in me; takes no offense at me

verse.note: The verb means to trip someone up or bring about their fall, and in the Gospels it usually refers to being turned away from trust or loyalty. 'Offended' now suggests hurt feelings, which is too weak. Some modern translations also use 'stumble' or 'fall away' here.

verse.text: As they were going away, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to look at? A reed shaken by the wind?

text.q: Then what did you go out to see? Someone dressed in soft clothes? Look, those who wear soft clothes are in the houses of kings.
Then why did you go out? To see a prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.
This is the one about whom it is written: ‘Look, I am sending my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way ahead of you.’

note.term: I am sending my messenger before your face

verse.note: The quotation follows Malachi 3:1, with wording that also echoes Exodus 23:20. The same book closes with a promise that God would send the prophet Elijah before the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5), which lies behind verse 14. 'Before your face' is a Hebrew idiom for 'ahead of you'.

text.q: Truly I tell you, among those born of women no one greater than John the Baptist has arisen; yet the least in the kingdom of the heavens is greater than he is.

verse.note: The Greek is plural, reflecting a Hebrew and Aramaic way of speaking that a first-century hearer would have noticed. Most translations flatten it to 'heaven'. The plural is kept here wherever Matthew uses it for God's dwelling.

text.q: From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of the heavens has been suffering violence, and the violent are seizing it.

note.traditional: suffers violence, and the violent take it by force

verse.note: This is one of the most disputed sentences in the Gospels. The verb can be passive ('suffers violence', that is, is attacked by opponents) or middle ('forces its way forward'), and those who 'seize' the kingdom may be enemies plundering it or eager people pressing into it. The rendering takes both clauses in the hostile sense, which fits the usually negative tone of the Greek words for 'violent people' and 'seize' and John's imprisonment in the context. The positive reading has serious scholarly support.

text.q: For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John,
and if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah, who is to come.
Let anyone who has ears hear.
But to what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplaces who call out to the others
and say, ‘We played the pipe for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not mourn.’
For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon.’
The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Look, a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ Yet wisdom is vindicated by her deeds.”

verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice, justify). Here the verb means to be shown to be in the right, which 'vindicated' says more clearly than 'justified'. Many modern translations have 'vindicated' or 'proved right'.

Many manuscripts read 'by her children', matching the parallel saying in Luke 7:35. The earliest witnesses to Matthew read 'deeds', and most editors think 'children' was introduced by copyists to bring Matthew into line with Luke. 'Deeds' picks up 'the deeds of the Messiah' in verse 2.

verse.text: Then he began to reproach the towns in which most of his miracles had taken place, because they had not turned back.
verse.note: 'Repent' now centres on feeling sorry. In the Gospels the word carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep 'repent' as an established term that readers understand to include a change of life.

text.q: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the miracles that took place in you had taken place in Tyre and Sidon, they would have turned back long ago in sackcloth and ashes.
But I tell you, it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you.
And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? No, you will go down to Hades. For if the miracles that took place in you had taken place in Sodom, it would have remained to this day.
But I tell you that it will be more bearable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment than for you.”

verse.text: At that time Jesus said, “I praise you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and intelligent and revealed them to little children.

text.q: Yes, Father, for this is what was pleasing in your sight.
Everything has been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.
Come to me, all you who toil and are burdened, and I will give you rest.
Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.

verse.note: 'Meek' now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes someone who is gentle and not self-assertive. 'Gentle' or 'humble' is the usual rendering in modern translations.

A yoke is the wooden frame that harnesses working animals to a load. In Jewish wisdom writing it was a familiar image for accepting instruction (Sirach 51:26 invites the reader to put their neck under wisdom's yoke), and later Jewish teachers spoke of the yoke of the Law. 'You will find rest for your souls' echoes Jeremiah 6:16.

text.q: For my yoke is easy to bear, and my burden is light.”

verse.text: At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath. His disciples were hungry, and they began to pluck heads of grain and eat.
But the Pharisees saw it and said to him, “Look, your disciples are doing what is not permitted on a Sabbath.”
He said to them, “Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, he and those with him:

text.q: how he entered the house of God, and they ate the loaves of presentation, which it was not permitted for him to eat, nor for those with him, but only for the priests?

note.traditional: the showbread / the bread of the Presence

verse.note: These are the twelve loaves set out each Sabbath on a table in the sanctuary and afterwards eaten only by priests (Leviticus 24:5–9); the David story is in 1 Samuel 21. The Greek phrase means 'the loaves of the setting-out'. 'Bread of the Presence', used by most modern translations, renders the Hebrew expression behind it rather than the Greek.

text.q: Or have you not read in the Law that on the Sabbath the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath and are guiltless?
I tell you that something greater than the temple is here.

verse.note: The Greek adjective is neuter, 'something greater', not masculine, 'someone greater'; some later manuscripts have the masculine, which lies behind older English versions. Most interpreters take the neuter as an indirect reference to Jesus himself or to the kingdom arriving in his work. The same neuter construction recurs in verses 41 and 42 with a different word, rendered 'something more'.

text.q: If you had known what this means, ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice,’ you would not have condemned the guiltless.
For the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.”

verse.text: Moving on from there, he went into their synagogue.
And there was a man with a withered hand. They questioned him, asking, “Is it permitted to heal on the Sabbath?” They asked this so that they might bring a charge against him.
He said to them, “Which of you, having a single sheep, if it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will not take hold of it and lift it out?

text.q: How much more valuable, then, is a person than a sheep! So it is permitted to do good on the Sabbath.”

verse.text: Then he said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He stretched it out, and it was restored, as sound as the other.
But the Pharisees went out and plotted against him, how they might destroy him.
Jesus, aware of this, withdrew from there. Many followed him, and he healed them all,
and he sternly ordered them not to make him known,
so that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled:

text.q: “Look, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved, in whom my soul delights. I will put my Spirit upon him, and he will announce justice to the Gentiles.

verse.note: The quotation is Isaiah 42:1–4, in a form that differs from the standard Greek version and is at points closer to the Hebrew. The Greek word can mean either 'servant' or 'child'; the Hebrew behind it means 'servant', and that is the usual rendering. The wording 'my beloved, in whom my soul delights' echoes the voice at Jesus's baptism (3:17).

The same Greek word is translated 'judgment' in verses 36, 41 and 42. Here and in verse 20 it stands for the Hebrew term in Isaiah that means right order or just rule, so most modern translations have 'justice'. Older versions have 'judgment', and some interpreters think Matthew does intend the announcement of a coming verdict.

Greek has one word for 'nations' and 'Gentiles'; in the plural it regularly means the non-Jewish peoples. 'The nations' would be an equally possible rendering here and in verse 21. Matthew's point is that Isaiah foresaw the servant's work reaching beyond Israel.

text.q: He will not quarrel or cry out, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets.
A bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not put out, until he brings justice through to victory.
And in his name the Gentiles will hope.”

verse.text: Then a demon-possessed man who was blind and mute was brought to him, and he healed him, so that the mute man could speak and see.
All the crowds were amazed and said, “Could this be the Son of David?”
But when the Pharisees heard it, they said, “This man does not drive out demons except by Beelzebul, the ruler of the demons.”
verse.note: A name for the ruler of the demons, whom verse 26 equates with Satan. Its origin is disputed. It may be connected with Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron in 2 Kings 1, and the spelling 'Beelzebub' in older English Bibles comes by way of the Latin tradition, not from the Greek manuscripts.

verse.text: Knowing their thoughts, he said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and no city or household divided against itself will stand.

text.q: And if Satan drives out Satan, he is divided against himself; how then will his kingdom stand?
And if I drive out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons drive them out? For this reason they themselves will be your judges.

verse.note: 'Sons' is a Semitic way of speaking of the members of a group, here probably exorcists belonging to the Pharisees' own circle, and need not mean their literal children. Jewish exorcism was a known practice in the period. The argument is that the charge against Jesus would condemn their own people as well.

text.q: But if it is by the Spirit of God that I drive out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.
Or how can anyone enter the strong man’s house and seize his goods unless he first ties up the strong man? Then he will plunder his house.
Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.
For this reason I tell you, people will be forgiven every sin and blasphemy, but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven.
And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the one to come.
Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree rotten and its fruit rotten; for the tree is known by its fruit.
Brood of vipers! How can you speak good things when you are evil? For out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks.
The good person brings good things out of a good store, and the evil person brings evil things out of an evil store.
But I tell you that for every idle word people speak, they will give an account on the day of judgment;
for by your words you will be vindicated, and by your words you will be condemned.”

verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two (righteous and just, righteousness and justice, justify). The verb here is courtroom language: to be declared in the right at the judgment, the opposite of 'condemned'. Most translations have 'justified' or 'acquitted'.

verse.text: Then some of the scribes and Pharisees responded to him, “Teacher, we want to see a sign from you.”
But he answered them, “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah the prophet.
verse.note: The word is used in the prophets' figurative sense, as in Hosea and Ezekiel, where Israel's unfaithfulness to God is pictured as a wife's unfaithfulness to her husband. It is not an accusation about sexual conduct.

text.q: For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea monster three days and three nights, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights.

verse.note: The Greek word means any huge sea creature and does not name a particular species. It is the word the Greek version of Jonah uses for the Hebrew 'great fish'. 'Whale' in older English Bibles is more specific than the Greek, and 'great fish' in many modern ones follows the Hebrew of Jonah instead of Matthew's word.

text.q: The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, because they turned back at Jonah’s proclamation, and look, something more than Jonah is here.

verse.note: 'Repent' now suggests mainly feeling sorry. The Greek word carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct, which is what the people of Nineveh do in Jonah 3. Most translations keep 'repented' as an established term understood to include a change of life.

text.q: The queen of the South will be raised at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and look, something more than Solomon is here.
When the unclean spirit comes out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, and does not find it.
Then it says, ‘I will return to my house, from which I came out.’ And when it comes, it finds the house unoccupied, swept, and put in order.

Then it goes and brings along with it seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they go in and settle there; and that person’s last state becomes worse than the first. So it will be also with this evil generation.”

verse.text: While he was still speaking to the crowds, there were his mother and his brothers, standing outside and seeking to speak to him.
Someone said to him, “Look, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking to speak to you.”
verse.note: Some early and important manuscripts lack this verse. It may have been dropped by accident, since it ends with the same Greek words as verse 46 and a copyist's eye could skip from one to the other. Verse 48 also presupposes that someone has spoken, so this edition prints the verse, though some editions bracket it as doubtful.

verse.text: But he replied to the one who told him, “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?”
And stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said, “Look, my mother and my brothers!

text.q: For whoever does the will of my Father in the heavens, that one is my brother and sister and mother.”

verse.note: The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase characteristic of Matthew that a first-century hearer would have noticed. Most translations flatten it to 'heaven'.

verse.text: That day Jesus went out of the house and sat beside the sea.
And large crowds gathered around him, so that he got into a boat and sat down, while the whole crowd stood on the shore.
And he told them many things in parables, saying: “Look, a sower went out to sow.

text.q: And as he sowed, some seeds fell along the path, and the birds came and ate them up.
Others fell on rocky ground, where they did not have much soil, and at once they sprang up, because they had no depth of soil;
but when the sun rose they were scorched, and because they had no root they withered.
Others fell among the thorns, and the thorns came up and choked them.
Still others fell on the good soil and produced grain: some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty.
Let the one who has ears hear.”

verse.text: The disciples came and said to him, “Why do you speak to them in parables?”
He answered them, “Because to you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of the heavens, but to them it has not been given.
verse.note: Matthew's Greek has the plural, 'the heavens', a Semitic turn of phrase that a first-century hearer would have noticed. Most translations flatten it to 'heaven'. The phrase is Matthew's usual equivalent of 'the kingdom of God' in the other Gospels.

text.q: For whoever has will be given more and will have an abundance; but whoever does not have, even what they have will be taken from them.
This is why I speak to them in parables: because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear or understand.
And in them the prophecy of Isaiah is being fulfilled, which says: ‘You will hear and hear but never understand, and you will look and look but never see.

verse.note: Verses 14–15 quote Isaiah 6:9–10, following the ancient Greek version (the Septuagint) almost word for word. In Isaiah the words belong to God's commissioning of the prophet, warning him that his message will meet a people unwilling to hear.

text.q: For this people’s heart has grown dull, and with their ears they have barely heard, and their eyes they have shut, so that they might never see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn back, and I would heal them.’
But blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear.
For truly I tell you, many prophets and righteous people longed to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it.
“You, then, hear the parable of the sower.
When anyone hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away what has been sown in that person’s heart. This is the one sown along the path.

note.term: the one sown along the path
note.traditional: this is what was sown along the path

verse.note: The Greek identifies the hearer with what is sown, although in the explanation the seed is the word. Some translations smooth this to 'the seed sown' or 'what was sown'. The masculine form here points to the person, so the slightly mixed image of the Greek is kept.

text.q: As for the one sown on rocky ground, this is the one who hears the word and at once receives it with joy,
yet has no root within and lasts only for a time; and when affliction or persecution comes because of the word, at once that person stumbles.

verse.note: The verb pictures being tripped or trapped, and in the Septuagint and the New Testament it is used for being brought to a fall in one's loyalty to God. Translations usually vary the English: 'falls away' here, 'causes of sin' in verse 41, 'took offense' in verse 57. One image is kept for the whole word-family in this chapter so that the link is visible.

text.q: As for the one sown among the thorns, this is the one who hears the word, but the anxiety of this age and the deceitfulness of wealth choke the word, and it becomes unfruitful.

note.traditional: the cares of this world; the worries of this life

verse.note: The Greek word is a time-word: the present era, set against the age to come. It is the same word as in 'the end of the age' (verses 39, 40, 49). Most modern translations have 'age' there but 'world' or 'life' here.

text.q: As for the one sown on the good soil, this is the one who hears the word and understands it, who indeed bears fruit and produces, in one case a hundredfold, in another sixty, in another thirty.”

verse.text: He set another parable before them: “The kingdom of the heavens may be compared to a man who sowed good seed in his field.

text.q: But while everyone was asleep, his enemy came and sowed weeds in among the wheat, and went away.

verse.note: The word names a particular weed, generally identified as darnel, a grass that looks much like wheat until the ears form. That is why the weeds only become visible in verse 26, and why pulling them out early would endanger the wheat.

text.q: When the plants sprouted and produced grain, then the weeds appeared as well.
The householder’s slaves came and said to him, ‘Master, did you not sow good seed in your field? Where then did the weeds come from?’

verse.note: The word denotes a person owned by a master, not a hired worker, and 'servant' softens this for a modern reader. Many recent translations and lexicons prefer 'slave'. Others keep 'servant' because ancient slavery differed in important ways from the later Atlantic slave trade.

text.q: He said to them, ‘An enemy has done this.’ The slaves said to him, ‘Then do you want us to go and collect them?’
But he said, ‘No, for in collecting the weeds you might uproot the wheat along with them.
Let both grow together until the harvest, and at harvest time I will say to the reapers, “Collect the weeds first and bind them in bundles to be burned, but gather the wheat into my barn.”’”

verse.text: He set another parable before them: “The kingdom of the heavens is like a mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his field.

text.q: It is the smallest of all the seeds, but when it has grown it is larger than the garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the sky come and nest in its branches.”

verse.note: Birds lodging in the branches of a great tree is an Old Testament image for a kingdom large enough to shelter the nations (Ezekiel 17:23; 31:6; Daniel 4:12). Mustard is a large garden shrub, not strictly a tree. Calling it one points the hearer to that background.

verse.text: He told them another parable: “The kingdom of the heavens is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour until it was all leavened.”
verse.note: The measure is the saton (Hebrew seah). Three of them is usually reckoned at something like 35–40 litres of flour, enough bread for well over a hundred people, so the amount is strikingly large. 'Hid' is the plain sense of the verb and fits the chapter's theme of hidden things (verses 35, 44).

verse.text: All these things Jesus spoke to the crowds in parables, and without a parable he would say nothing to them,
so that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden from the foundation.”

note.traditional: from the foundation of the world

verse.note: The quotation is Psalm 78:2. Many manuscripts read 'from the foundation of the world'. SBLGNT prints the shorter text without 'of the world', though that is still the sense. A few manuscripts read 'through Isaiah the prophet', which is generally judged not to be original.

verse.text: Then he left the crowds and went into the house. And his disciples came to him and said, “Explain to us the parable of the weeds in the field.”
He answered, “The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man.

text.q: The field is the world. As for the good seed, these are the sons of the kingdom. The weeds are the sons of the evil one,

verse.note: 'Son of' is a Semitic way of saying 'belonging to' or 'sharing the character of', and is not limited to males. Many translations have 'children' or 'people of the kingdom'. 'Of the evil one' could grammatically be 'of evil', but verse 19 and the devil's role in verse 39 favor the personal sense.

text.q: and the enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels.
So just as the weeds are collected and burned with fire, so it will be at the end of the age.
The Son of Man will send out his angels, and they will collect out of his kingdom everything that causes stumbling and those who practice lawlessness,
and they will throw them into the furnace of fire. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
Then the righteous will shine out like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. Let the one who has ears hear.
“The kingdom of the heavens is like treasure hidden in the field, which a man found and hid; and in his joy he goes and sells everything he has and buys that field.
“Again, the kingdom of the heavens is like a merchant looking for fine pearls.
On finding one pearl of great value, he went away and sold everything he had and bought it.
“Again, the kingdom of the heavens is like a dragnet that was thrown into the sea and gathered fish of every kind.
When it was full, they hauled it up onto the shore, sat down, and collected the good ones into containers, but threw the bad ones away.
So it will be at the end of the age. The angels will go out and separate the evil from among the righteous
and throw them into the furnace of fire. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

verse.text: “Have you understood all these things?” They said to him, “Yes.”
And he said to them, “For this reason every scribe who has become a disciple of the kingdom of the heavens is like a householder who brings out of his storeroom things new and old.”

note.term: who has become a disciple of
note.traditional: instructed unto the kingdom; trained for the kingdom

verse.note: The verb is the cognate of 'disciple' and can mean either 'become a disciple' or 'be made a disciple, be instructed'. The following dative can be taken as 'of', 'for' or 'in' the kingdom. Many translations have 'trained for the kingdom'; this rendering keeps the link with the disciples who have just said they understand.

verse.text: Now when Jesus had finished these parables, he moved on from there.
He came to his hometown and taught them in their synagogue, so that they were astonished and said, “Where did this man get this wisdom and these mighty works?

text.q: Is this not the carpenter’s son? Is his mother not called Mary, and his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas?

verse.note: The Greek word covers a craftsman who builds, most often in wood but also in other materials. 'Builder' or 'woodworker' would also be defensible. 'Carpenter' is kept as the nearest single English trade.

text.q: And his sisters, are they not all here with us? Where then did this man get all these things?”

verse.text: And they stumbled over him. But Jesus said to them, “A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown and in his own house.”
And he did not do many mighty works there, because of their unbelief.
At that time Herod the tetrarch heard the report about Jesus,
verse.note: This is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea under Roman oversight. 'Tetrarch' was the title of a ruler of part of a divided kingdom and ranked below a king.

verse.text: and he said to his attendants, “This is John the Baptist. He has been raised from the dead, and that is why these powers are at work in him.”
For Herod had seized John, bound him, and put him away in prison on account of Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip,

note.term: the wife of his brother Philip

verse.note: Herodias had left her first husband, a half-brother of Antipas, to marry Antipas. Jewish law forbade marrying a brother's wife while the brother was alive (Leviticus 18:16; 20:21), which is the basis of John's charge in verse 4. Josephus calls the first husband simply Herod; whether he also bore the name Philip is disputed.

verse.text: for John had been telling him, “It is not lawful for you to have her.”
And although he wanted to kill him, he feared the crowd, because they regarded him as a prophet.
But when Herod’s birthday celebration came, the daughter of Herodias danced before the company and pleased Herod,
so much that he promised with an oath to give her whatever she asked.
Prompted by her mother, she said, “Give me, here on a platter, the head of John the Baptist.”
The king was distressed, but because of his oaths and his dinner guests he ordered it to be given,
verse.note: Antipas never officially held the title of king, and Matthew has called him tetrarch in verse 1. 'King' here reflects popular usage for a local ruler rather than his formal rank.

verse.text: and he sent and had John beheaded in the prison.
His head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and she brought it to her mother.
His disciples came and took away the corpse and buried him, and they went and told Jesus.
When Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there in a boat to a remote place by himself. But the crowds heard of it and followed him on foot from the towns.
When he came ashore he saw a large crowd, and he was moved with compassion for them and healed their sick.
When evening came, the disciples approached him and said, “This is a remote place, and the hour is already late. Send the crowds away, so that they can go into the villages and buy themselves food.”
But Jesus said to them, “They do not need to go away. You give them something to eat.”
They said to him, “We have nothing here except five loaves and two fish.”
He said, “Bring them here to me.”

Then he ordered the crowds to recline on the grass. He took the five loaves and the two fish, looked up to heaven and said the blessing; then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds.
verse.note: The Greek verb means to lie back or recline, the normal posture at a meal in the first century. Most translations say 'sit down', which is the modern equivalent but loses the suggestion that the crowd is being arranged as for a meal.

The Greek verb has no object here. Some translations supply one, so that Jesus blesses the loaves; others render it 'gave thanks'. The Jewish custom at meals was to bless God for the food, and that is the more likely sense, though the Greek does not settle it.

verse.text: They all ate and were satisfied, and they picked up what was left over of the broken pieces: twelve baskets full.
Those who ate were about five thousand men, besides women and children.
Immediately he made the disciples get into the boat and go ahead of him to the other side, while he sent the crowds away.
After sending the crowds away, he went up the mountain by himself to pray. When evening came, he was there alone.
The boat was already a long way from the land, battered by the waves, for the wind was against it.

note.term: a long way from the land
note.traditional: in the midst of the sea

verse.note: The Greek says the boat was 'many stadia' from land. A stadion was roughly 185 metres (about 600 feet), so the distance is probably a few miles. Other manuscripts read 'in the middle of the sea', as in Mark's account, and older English versions follow that reading.

verse.text: In the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea.

note.term: the fourth watch of the night
note.traditional: the fourth watch of the night

verse.note: On the Roman reckoning the night was divided into four watches. The fourth ran from about three in the morning until dawn, so the disciples had been struggling at sea for most of the night.

verse.text: When the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were terrified and said, “It is a ghost!” And they cried out in fear.
But at once Jesus spoke to them: “Take courage; it is I. Do not be afraid.”
verse.note: The Greek is literally 'I am', the ordinary way of saying 'It's me'. The same words are also God's self-designation in the Greek Old Testament (for example in Exodus 3:14 and Isaiah 43:10). Many interpreters hear that echo here, in a scene where Jesus walks on the sea as God does in Job 9:8; the plain sense of self-identification is certain, the further resonance is likely but debated.

verse.text: Peter answered him, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the waters.”
He said, “Come.” And Peter got down from the boat, walked on the waters, and came toward Jesus.
But seeing the strong wind, he became afraid, and beginning to sink he cried out, “Lord, save me!”
verse.note: Some important early manuscripts lack the word 'strong' and read simply 'seeing the wind'. The edition translated here includes it; the sense is little affected either way.

verse.text: Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, took hold of him, and said to him, “You of little faith, why did you doubt?”
And when they got into the boat, the wind dropped.
Those in the boat bowed down before him, saying, “Truly you are God’s Son.”
verse.note: The Greek verb denotes the act of bowing or prostrating oneself in homage, whether before a god, a king or a superior. Most translations render it 'worshiped' here, and the accompanying confession shows that the homage is of the highest kind. The rendering keeps the physical act the word describes and lets the confession carry its meaning.

verse.text: When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret.
The men of that place recognized him and sent word throughout that whole surrounding region, and people brought to him all who were ill,
and they begged him to let them touch just the fringe of his cloak. And all who touched it were made well.
verse.note: The word can mean the edge of a garment, but it is also the term for the tassels that Jewish men wore on the corners of their outer garment in obedience to Numbers 15:38–39. Matthew uses it for those tassels in 23:5, so that is probably what is meant here.

verse.text: Then Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus from Jerusalem and said,

text.q: “Why do your disciples break the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat bread.”

verse.note: This refers to a body of rulings handed down by earlier teachers and treated by the Pharisees as binding alongside the written Law. The handwashing at issue was a matter of ritual purity, not hygiene; the Law of Moses does not require it of ordinary people before meals. “Eat bread” is a Semitic way of saying “have a meal.”

verse.text: He answered them, “And why do you yourselves break the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition?

text.q: For God said, ‘Honor your father and mother,’ and, ‘Whoever speaks ill of father or mother must be put to death.’
But you say, ‘Whoever says to his father or mother, “Whatever help you might have had from me is an offering,”

verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary Septuagint term for something offered to God; Mark’s parallel gives the Hebrew word, korban. A person could vow that property was dedicated in this way, which put it out of other people’s reach. Jesus’ charge is that the tradition let such a vow override the duty to support one’s parents.

text.q: is not to honor his father.’ So you have nullified the word of God for the sake of your tradition.

note.term: is not to honor his father

verse.note: The Greek is an emphatic negative, literally “will certainly not honor,” in a sentence that is grammatically broken off. Most translations soften it to “need not honor,” a release from obligation. It can equally be read as the wording of the ruling itself, which holds the son to his vow and so forbids him to help; the rendering here keeps that stronger sense. “Honor” in this context includes material support.
Manuscripts vary here between “the word,” “the law” and “the commandment” of God; the sense is little affected. Many manuscripts also add “or his mother” after “his father.”

text.q: Hypocrites! Isaiah prophesied well about you when he said,
‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far away from me;
they worship me in vain, teaching human commands as doctrines.’”

verse.text: And calling the crowd to him, he said to them, “Listen and understand:

text.q: it is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth, this defiles a person.”

verse.note: The Greek verb literally means “to make common.” In Jewish Greek it had become a technical term for making someone or something ritually unclean, unfit for contact with what is holy. The dispute is about purity before God, not about dirt or health.

verse.text: Then the disciples came and said to him, “Do you know that the Pharisees took offense when they heard this saying?”
He answered, “Every plant that my heavenly Father did not plant will be uprooted.

text.q: Leave them; they are blind guides of the blind. And if a blind person guides a blind person, both will fall into a pit.”

verse.text: Peter answered him, “Explain this parable to us.”
He said, “Are even you still without understanding?

text.q: Do you not see that everything that goes into the mouth passes into the stomach and is expelled into the latrine?
But the things that come out of the mouth come from the heart, and those defile a person.
For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, acts of sexual immorality, thefts, false testimonies, slanders.
These are the things that defile a person; but eating with unwashed hands does not defile a person.”

verse.text: And leaving there, Jesus withdrew to the region of Tyre and Sidon.
And look, a Canaanite woman from that territory came out and kept crying, “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David! My daughter is severely tormented by a demon.”

note.traditional: a woman of Canaan / a Canaanite woman

verse.note: “Canaanite” was an archaic term by the first century; Mark’s parallel calls her a Greek, Syrophoenician by birth. Matthew’s word recalls the ancient inhabitants of the land in Israel’s Scriptures and marks her plainly as a Gentile outsider, which sharpens the exchange that follows.

verse.text: But he did not answer her a word. And his disciples came and kept asking him, “Send her away, because she keeps crying out after us.”
He answered, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”
But she came and bowed down before him, saying, “Lord, help me.”
verse.note: The verb describes the physical act of bowing or prostrating oneself before a superior, whether a god, a king, or someone whose help is being begged. Older versions have “worshiped”; most modern versions have “knelt.” Here it is the gesture of a desperate petitioner, and the text does not say how much more she meant by it.

verse.text: He answered, “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the little dogs.”
verse.note: The Greek uses a diminutive form, not the ordinary word for dog. Diminutives had often lost their force in the Greek of this period, so “dogs” is a possible rendering; but the picture of animals under the family table suggests household dogs, not street scavengers. Whether the diminutive softens the saying is debated; “dogs” was in any case a term Jews could use for Gentiles.

verse.text: She said, “Yes, Lord, for even the little dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.”
verse.note: Most translations have “Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs,” as though she were objecting. The Greek connective means “for indeed” or “for even,” not “but.” She accepts his image and argues from within it: the dogs get fed too, without the children losing their bread. The word for “masters” is the plural of the word she uses to address Jesus as “Lord.”

verse.text: Then Jesus answered her, “O woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you wish.” And her daughter was healed from that hour.
Moving on from there, Jesus went along beside the Sea of Galilee, and he went up the mountain and sat down there.
Large crowds came to him, bringing with them people who were mute, blind, lame, crippled, and many others, and they set them down at his feet, and he healed them,
so that the crowd was amazed when they saw the mute speaking, the crippled made sound, the lame walking, and the blind seeing. And they glorified the God of Israel.

Jesus called his disciples to him and said, “I have compassion on the crowd, because they have stayed with me three days now and have nothing to eat. I do not want to send them away hungry, or they may collapse on the way.”
The disciples said to him, “Where in a deserted place could we get so many loaves as to satisfy so large a crowd?”
Jesus said to them, “How many loaves do you have?” They said, “Seven, and a few small fish.”
And directing the crowd to recline on the ground,
he took the seven loaves and the fish, and after giving thanks he broke them and kept giving them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds.
They all ate and were satisfied, and they picked up what was left over of the broken pieces, seven baskets full.
verse.note: This is a different Greek word from the “baskets” of the feeding of the five thousand (14:20). It denotes a larger hamper, the kind in which Paul was lowered from the wall of Damascus (Acts 9:25). Matthew keeps the two words distinct when Jesus recalls both feedings in 16:9–10.

verse.text: Those who ate were four thousand men, besides women and children.
And after sending the crowds away, he got into the boat and went to the territory of Magadan.
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read Magadan, a place otherwise unknown. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read Magdala, a known town on the western shore of the lake. Mark’s parallel has Dalmanutha, which is equally obscure.

verse.text: The Pharisees and Sadducees came to him and, testing him, asked him to show them a sign from heaven.
verse.note: The Greek word here is the same one translated “sky” in verses 2 and 3. It means both the visible sky and the dwelling of God. The request is for a sign from God, perhaps one seen in the sky, and Jesus’ reply plays on the double meaning, which English cannot keep with a single word.

verse.text: He answered them, “When evening comes, you say, ‘Fair weather, for the sky is red,’
verse.note: The weather saying, from these words to the end of verse 3, is absent from several of the earliest and most important manuscripts. Many scholars think it was added early, perhaps under the influence of Luke 12:54–56. Others think copyists dropped it in regions where a red morning sky does not signal rain. The SBLGNT prints it without brackets, and it is translated here.

text.q: and in the morning, ‘Stormy today, for the sky is red and overcast.’ You know how to interpret the face of the sky, but the signs of the times you cannot.

verse.text: An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah.” And he left them and went away.
When the disciples came to the other side, they had forgotten to bring bread.
Jesus said to them, “Watch out, and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.”
They began discussing this among themselves, saying, “We brought no bread.”

note.traditional: It is because we have taken no bread

verse.note: The Greek word introducing the disciples’ words can either mark a quotation or mean “because”. Many translations take it the second way: “It is because we brought no bread.” Either way the disciples have taken the remark about leaven as a comment on their forgotten provisions.

verse.text: Aware of this, Jesus said, “You of little faith, why are you discussing among yourselves that you brought no bread?

text.q: Do you not yet see? Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you collected?
Or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many large baskets you collected?
How do you not see that I was not speaking to you about bread? But beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.”

verse.text: Then they understood that he had not told them to beware of the leaven of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.
When Jesus came into the region of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, “Who do people say the Son of Man is?”
They said, “Some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, and still others Jeremiah or one of the prophets.”
He said to them, “But you, who do you say I am?”
Simon Peter answered, “You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God.”
verse.note: The Greek christos translates the Hebrew title for the anointed king Israel expected. Here, and in verse 20, it is a title under discussion and not yet a name, and “Messiah” conveys that to a modern reader. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels and keep “Christ” where it works as a name.

verse.text: Jesus answered him, “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, for flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father who is in the heavens.
verse.note: The Greek is plural here and in verse 19, as usually in Matthew’s phrases “Father in the heavens” and “kingdom of the heavens”. The plural reflects Hebrew and Aramaic usage. Most translations flatten it to “heaven”, and this translation keeps it.

text.q: And I in turn tell you: you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hades will not overpower it.

note.term: you are Peter, and on this rock

verse.note: The Greek plays on the name Peter (Petros) and the word for rock (petra). In Aramaic the two were probably the same word, kepha. Whether “this rock” is Peter himself, his confession, or Christ has long been disputed along confessional lines. Most modern scholars of all traditions take it to refer to Peter.

The Greek word meant a gathering of citizens, and in the Septuagint it is the term for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation to keep the sense a first-century hearer would have caught.

Hades is the realm of the dead, not the place of final punishment. “The gates of Hades” is a Septuagint expression for death and its power (for example Isaiah 38:10). The promise is most likely that death will not overcome the community. Some interpreters instead see the forces of evil attacking it.

text.q: I will give you the keys of the kingdom of the heavens, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound in the heavens, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in the heavens.”

note.term: will be bound in the heavens

verse.note: “Binding” and “loosing” match terms known from later rabbinic usage for forbidding and permitting conduct, and possibly for excluding from and readmitting to the community. The Greek construction can also be read “will have been bound” and “will have been loosed”, which would make heaven’s decision come before Peter’s rather than ratify it. The grammar is disputed. The rendering here describes the resulting state without settling the order.

verse.text: Then he ordered the disciples to tell no one that he was the Messiah.
From then on Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.
Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying, “God forbid, Lord! This will never happen to you.”

note.traditional: Far be it from you, Lord

verse.note: The Greek is literally “merciful to you”, short for “may God be merciful to you”. In the Septuagint the expression renders a Hebrew idiom of strong refusal, “far be it”. It is a vehement protest, not a blessing.

verse.text: But he turned and said to Peter, “Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, because your mind is not on the things of God but on the things of people.”
verse.note: “Satan” is a Hebrew word meaning adversary, and Peter is addressed as playing the tempter’s part; compare Jesus’ dismissal of the devil in 4:10. “Behind me” is the same Greek phrase translated “after me” in verse 24. Peter is being sent back to the disciple’s place, following behind Jesus and not blocking his path.

verse.text: Then Jesus said to his disciples, “If anyone wants to come after me, they must deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow me.

text.q: For whoever wants to save their life will lose it, but whoever loses their life for my sake will find it.
For what good will it do a person if they gain the whole world but forfeit their life? Or what will a person give in exchange for their life?

verse.note: The Greek word is the same one translated “life” in verse 25, and the argument depends on its being the same. It means a person’s life or self, not an immaterial part as distinct from the body. Many older translations switch to “soul” in this verse; a number of modern ones keep “life”.

text.q: For the Son of Man is going to come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will repay each person according to what they have done.
Truly I tell you, there are some of those standing here who will certainly not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.”

verse.note: What event is meant is disputed. Proposals include the transfiguration that follows immediately in chapter 17, Jesus’ resurrection and exaltation, the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, and the final coming of the Son of Man. The translation leaves the question open, as the Greek does.

verse.text: Six days later Jesus took with him Peter, James, and John his brother, and led them up a high mountain by themselves.
And he was transformed in front of them: his face shone like the sun, and his clothes became white as the light.
verse.note: The traditional 'transfigured' comes from the Latin Bible and survives in English almost only for this event. The Greek verb is an ordinary word for a change of form or appearance, and the same verb is usually rendered 'transformed' in Romans 12:2 and 2 Corinthians 3:18. 'Transformed' gives the plain sense a first-century reader would have heard.

verse.text: And suddenly Moses and Elijah appeared to them, talking with him.
Peter spoke up and said to Jesus, “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you wish, I will put up three shelters here, one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.”
verse.note: The word means a tent or temporary hut. It is the Septuagint's term both for the wilderness tabernacle and for the booths of the Feast of Booths, and many interpreters hear an echo of that festival in Peter's offer. Some manuscripts read 'let us make' rather than 'I will make'.

verse.text: While he was still speaking, a bright cloud suddenly overshadowed them, and a voice came from the cloud, saying, “This is my Son, the beloved, with whom I am well pleased. Listen to him!”
verse.note: The voice repeats the words spoken at Jesus's baptism (Matthew 3:17) and adds a command. Most interpreters hear an echo of Deuteronomy 18:15, where Moses promises a prophet like himself and says, 'you shall listen to him'. With Moses and Elijah present, the command singles out Jesus as the one to be heeded.

verse.text: When the disciples heard this, they fell on their faces and were terrified.
Jesus came and touched them and said, “Get up, and do not be afraid.”
And when they looked up, they saw no one but Jesus himself, alone.
As they were coming down from the mountain, Jesus commanded them, “Tell no one about the vision until the Son of Man has been raised from the dead.”
The disciples asked him, “Why then do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?”
verse.note: The expectation rests on Malachi 4:5–6, where God promises to send the prophet Elijah before the day of the Lord to restore the hearts of fathers and children. Jesus's reply in verse 11 uses the same verb, 'restore', that the Greek version of Malachi uses.

verse.text: He answered, “Elijah does come, and he will restore everything.

text.q: But I tell you that Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but did to him whatever they wanted. In the same way the Son of Man too is about to suffer at their hands.”

verse.text: Then the disciples understood that he had spoken to them about John the Baptist.
When they came to the crowd, a man approached him, knelt before him,
and said, “Lord, have mercy on my son, for he has seizures and suffers terribly; he often falls into the fire, and often into the water.
verse.note: The Greek verb is literally 'is moonstruck', reflecting the ancient belief that recurring seizures were tied to the phases of the moon. The symptoms described fit what is now called epilepsy, and many modern versions say 'epileptic'. 'Has seizures' describes the condition without importing either the ancient theory or a modern diagnosis; verse 18 attributes the boy's condition to a demon.

text.q: I brought him to your disciples, and they could not heal him.”

verse.text: Jesus answered, “O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you? How long am I to put up with you? Bring him here to me.”
verse.note: The word describes something bent out of shape and so morally distorted. 'Perverse' is the usual rendering, but in current English it tends to suggest either mere contrariness or sexual deviance. The phrase echoes Deuteronomy 32:5 in the Greek version, where Moses calls Israel a 'crooked and twisted generation'.

verse.text: Jesus rebuked the demon, and it came out of him, and the boy was healed from that very hour.
verse.note: The Greek says only 'Jesus rebuked him/it, and the demon came out of him'. The pronoun could refer to the boy or to the demon. Most translations take it as the demon, since 'rebuke' is the usual verb for Jesus's commands to unclean spirits, and the translation makes that explicit.

verse.text: Then the disciples came to Jesus privately and said, “Why could we not drive it out?”

He said to them, “Because of your little faith. For truly I tell you, if you have faith like a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move, and nothing will be impossible for you.”

note.term: nothing will be impossible for you

verse.note: Verse 21 of the traditional numbering ('But this kind does not come out except by prayer and fasting') is absent from the earliest manuscripts and is not printed in the Greek text translated here. It is generally thought to have been added by copyists from the parallel in Mark 9:29. Some manuscripts also read 'unbelief' rather than 'little faith' earlier in this verse.

verse.text: As they were gathering in Galilee, Jesus said to them, “The Son of Man is about to be handed over into human hands,
verse.note: The Greek plays on a single word: the 'Son of Man' (literally 'son of the human being') is to be handed over into the hands of 'human beings'. The word refers to people in general rather than males, and 'human hands' keeps something of the echo. The verb 'handed over' is the same one elsewhere rendered 'betrayed' or 'delivered'.

verse.text: and they will kill him, and on the third day he will be raised.” And they were deeply grieved.
When they came to Capernaum, the collectors of the two-drachma tax approached Peter and said, “Your teacher pays the two-drachma tax, doesn’t he?”
verse.note: This was the annual contribution of two drachmas, equal to a half-shekel, paid by adult Jewish men for the upkeep of the Jerusalem temple, on the basis of Exodus 30:13. It was not a Roman tax. This explains Jesus's argument in verses 25–26: the tax is owed to God, and a king's sons do not pay their father's tax.

verse.text: He said, “Yes.” And when he came into the house, Jesus spoke to him first: “What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth collect tolls or poll tax, from their own sons or from others?”
verse.note: The 'sons' may be the king's own family, as opposed to everyone else, or the king's own people, as opposed to subject foreigners. Most interpreters take it as the royal family, which fits the application: Jesus, and by extension his disciples, stand to God as sons, not as taxpayers. 'Sons' is kept so that the link with 'my Son' in verse 5 remains audible.

verse.text: When he said, “From others,” Jesus said to him, “Then the sons are free.

text.q: But so that we do not give them offense, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up. When you open its mouth you will find a four-drachma coin; take that and give it to them for me and for you.”

note.traditional: a piece of money (KJV); a shekel

verse.note: The Greek names a specific coin, the stater, worth four drachmas. That is exactly the two-drachma tax for two people, which is why it covers both Jesus and Peter.

verse.text: At that time the disciples came to Jesus and said, “Who then is greatest in the kingdom of the heavens?”
verse.note: The Greek is plural here and in Matthew's phrase 'Father in the heavens', reflecting a Hebrew and Aramaic way of speaking that a first-century hearer would have recognised. Most translations flatten it to 'heaven'. This translation keeps the plural wherever the Greek has it; verse 18, where the Greek is singular, reads 'heaven'.

verse.text: He called a child to him, stood the child in their midst,
and said, “Truly I tell you, unless you turn and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of the heavens.

text.q: So whoever humbles himself like this child, that is the one who is greatest in the kingdom of the heavens.
And whoever welcomes one such child in my name welcomes me.
But whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him to have a donkey's millstone hung around his neck and to be drowned in the depths of the sea.

note.traditional: offend (KJV); cause to sin (many modern versions)

verse.note: The verb and its noun (rendered 'stumbling blocks' in verse 7) come from the image of a trap or an obstacle that brings someone down. In Jewish Greek they describe whatever causes a person to fall away from God. 'Offend' now suggests hurt feelings, and 'cause to sin' is narrower than the Greek. Several modern translations also use 'stumble'.

The Greek specifies the large upper stone of a mill turned by a donkey, as distinct from the small hand mill used in a household. Most translations say 'a great millstone' or 'a heavy millstone'. The point is the stone's size.

text.q: Woe to the world because of stumbling blocks! For stumbling blocks must come, but woe to the person through whom the stumbling block comes!

If your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you. It is better for you to enter life maimed or lame than to have two hands or two feet and be thrown into the eternal fire.
And if your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you. It is better for you to enter life with one eye than to have two eyes and be thrown into the Gehenna of fire.

verse.note: Gehenna is a place name, the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, which by this period had become the name for the place of final fiery judgment. Many translations render it 'hell', usually with a footnote. That merges it with Hades and with later imagery, so the name is kept here.

text.q: See that you do not look down on one of these little ones, for I tell you that their angels in the heavens continually see the face of my Father who is in the heavens.

note.term: see the face of my Father

verse.note: To 'see the face' of a king was a court expression for having direct access to his presence. The saying means that the angels who represent these little ones stand in the highest rank before God. It reflects a Jewish belief in angels assigned to peoples or individuals. The verse does not spell out how that guardianship works.

note.term: my Father who is in the heavens

verse.note: The verse numbering passes from 10 to 12. Verse 11 ('For the Son of Man came to save what was lost') is absent from the earliest manuscripts. It is widely judged to be a later addition drawn from Luke 19:10, and the Greek text translated here omits it.

text.q: What do you think? If someone has a hundred sheep and one of them goes astray, will he not leave the ninety-nine on the hills and go and search for the one that is straying?
And if he does find it, truly I tell you, he rejoices over it more than over the ninety-nine that never went astray.
In the same way, it is not the will of your Father who is in the heavens that one of these little ones should perish.
If your brother sins against you, go and show him his fault, between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have won your brother.

verse.note: The words 'against you' are missing from two of the oldest major manuscripts, and some editions and translations omit or bracket them. Without them the saying concerns any sin by a fellow believer, not only a personal wrong. The Greek text translated here includes them, and the question is disputed.

text.q: But if he does not listen, take one or two others with you, so that ‘by the mouth of two witnesses or three every matter may be established.’

note.term: by the mouth of two witnesses or three every matter may be established

verse.note: Jesus is citing the rule of evidence in Deuteronomy 19:15, which required more than one witness before a charge could stand. 'By the mouth of' is the Hebrew idiom for 'on the testimony of'.

text.q: If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the assembly; and if he refuses to listen even to the assembly, let him be to you like a Gentile and a tax collector.

verse.note: The Greek word meant a gathering of citizens, and in the Greek Old Testament it was the term for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation; here it means the local gathered community of disciples.

text.q: Truly I tell you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.

verse.note: The Greek form can also be read 'will have been bound' and 'will have been loosed', which would make the community's decision follow one already made in heaven. Most translations use the simple future, as here, and grammarians disagree on how much weight the form carries. 'Bind' and 'loose' were Jewish terms for forbidding and permitting, or for imposing and lifting a ban. The 'you' is plural.

text.q: Again, truly I tell you that if two of you agree on earth about any matter they ask for, it will be done for them by my Father who is in the heavens.
For where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst.”

verse.text: Then Peter came up and said to him, “Lord, how many times shall my brother sin against me and I forgive him? Up to seven times?”
Jesus said to him, “I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy-seven times.
verse.note: The Greek can be read as either 'seventy-seven times' or 'seventy times seven' (490). The identical phrase stands in the Greek version of Genesis 4:24 for Lamech's seventy-sevenfold vengeance, which Jesus appears to be reversing, so 'seventy-seven' is preferred here. Either way the number means forgiveness without keeping count.

text.q: For this reason the kingdom of the heavens may be compared to a king who wanted to settle accounts with his slaves.

verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master, and the story assumes it: the king can order the man and his family sold. 'Servants' is the traditional rendering and some modern versions keep it. A king's slaves could hold high office and handle great sums, as this one evidently does.

text.q: When he began to settle them, a man was brought to him who owed ten thousand talents.

verse.note: A talent was the largest unit of money, worth roughly six thousand denarii, and a denarius was about a day's wage for a labourer. 'Ten thousand' is the highest number for which Greek had a single word, so the sum is deliberately beyond imagining. The hundred denarii of verse 28 is a real debt of a few months' wages, yet it is hundreds of thousands of times smaller.

text.q: Since he had no means to repay, the master ordered him to be sold, with his wife and children and everything he had, and repayment to be made.
So the slave fell down and bowed low before him, saying, ‘Be patient with me, and I will repay you everything.’
Moved with compassion, the master of that slave released him and forgave him the loan.
But that slave went out and found one of his fellow slaves who owed him a hundred denarii. He seized him and began to choke him, saying, ‘Repay what you owe.’
So his fellow slave fell down and pleaded with him, saying, ‘Be patient with me, and I will repay you.’
But he refused. Instead he went and threw him into prison until he repaid what was owed.
When his fellow slaves saw what had happened, they were deeply distressed, and they went and reported to their master everything that had happened.
Then his master summoned him and said to him, ‘You wicked slave! I forgave you all that debt because you pleaded with me.
Should you not also have had mercy on your fellow slave, as I had mercy on you?’
And in his anger his master handed him over to the torturers until he repaid all that was owed.
So also my heavenly Father will do to you, unless each of you forgives his brother from your hearts.”

verse.text: When Jesus had finished these sayings, he left Galilee and came into the region of Judea beyond the Jordan.
Large crowds followed him, and he healed them there.
Some Pharisees came to him to test him, asking, “Is it permitted for a man to divorce his wife for any reason whatever?”
verse.note: The question reflects a live debate over the grounds for divorce in Deuteronomy 24:1. Later rabbinic sources record that the school of Shammai limited divorce to sexual misconduct, while the school of Hillel allowed it for almost any cause. The Pharisees are asking Jesus to take a side; the phrase could also be read more narrowly as 'for every kind of reason'.

verse.text: He answered, “Have you not read that the Creator from the beginning ‘made them male and female’

text.q: and said, ‘For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two will become one flesh’?
So they are no longer two but one flesh. What God has joined together, then, let no human being separate.”

verse.text: They said to him, “Why then did Moses command us to give a certificate of dismissal and divorce her?”
He said to them, “It was because of your hardness of heart that Moses permitted you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it has not been so.

text.q: And I tell you, whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another commits adultery, and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.”

verse.note: The Greek word is a broad term for unlawful sexual activity, and its exact scope here is disputed. Most interpreters take it to mean adultery or sexual unfaithfulness by the wife. Others limit it to unchastity before marriage, or to marriages within the degrees of kinship forbidden in Leviticus 18. The broad English term leaves the question as open as the Greek does.

note.term: and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery

verse.note: This final clause is absent from some important early manuscripts and is omitted by several modern critical editions and translations. Those editions regard it as an addition by copyists influenced by Matthew 5:32. The SBLGNT, followed here, includes it.

verse.text: The disciples said to him, “If that is how things stand between a man and his wife, it is better not to marry.”
But he said to them, “Not everyone can accept this saying, but only those to whom it has been given.
verse.note: It is unclear which saying is meant. It may be the disciples' remark that it is better not to marry, in which case Jesus grants that celibacy is a gift for some. It may instead be his own teaching on marriage and divorce in verses 4–9. Most interpreters prefer the first, since verse 12 goes on to speak of those who forgo marriage.

text.q: For there are eunuchs who were born that way from their mother’s womb, and there are eunuchs who were made eunuchs by people, and there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of the heavens. Let the one who can accept it accept it.”

verse.note: Eunuchs were a familiar class in the ancient world, some of them castrated to serve in royal courts. The third group is almost universally understood as a figure of speech for those who choose to remain unmarried for the sake of God's kingdom. It is not taken as a reference to physical self-mutilation.

The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase that follows Hebrew and Aramaic usage and is characteristic of Matthew. Most translations flatten it to 'heaven'. The plural is kept here because a first-century hearer would have noticed it; the phrase means the same as 'the kingdom of God' in verse 24.

verse.text: Then children were brought to him so that he might lay his hands on them and pray, but the disciples rebuked them.
But Jesus said, “Let the children be, and do not stop them from coming to me, for the kingdom of the heavens belongs to such as these.”
And after laying his hands on them, he went on from there.
Just then someone came up to him and said, “Teacher, what good thing must I do to have eternal life?”
verse.note: In Jewish usage of the period, 'eternal life' is the life of the age to come, the era of God's reign that follows the present age. The phrase concerns the kind of life as well as its unending length, which is why Jesus can call it simply 'life' in verse 17. 'Eternal' is the standard rendering; a minority of translators render 'life of the age to come'.

verse.text: He said to him, “Why do you ask me about what is good? There is only one who is good. But if you want to enter into life, keep the commandments.”

note.term: Why do you ask me about what is good?
note.traditional: Why callest thou me good? there is none good but one, that is, God

verse.note: Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read 'Good Teacher' in verse 16 and 'Why do you call me good? No one is good except one, God' here. That wording matches the parallel accounts in Mark 10 and Luke 18. The earliest manuscripts of Matthew have the form translated here, and the longer form is generally regarded as a harmonization by copyists.

verse.text: He said to him, “Which ones?” Jesus said, “‘You shall not murder,’ ‘You shall not commit adultery,’ ‘You shall not steal,’ ‘You shall not give false testimony,’

text.q: ‘Honor your father and mother,’ and ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’”

verse.text: The young man said to him, “All these I have observed. What do I still lack?”
Jesus said to him, “If you want to be complete, go, sell what you own and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in the heavens. Then come, follow me.”
verse.note: The Greek word describes something that has reached its goal: whole, mature, lacking nothing. In the Greek Old Testament it translates Hebrew words for wholehearted or undivided devotion. 'Perfect', the usual rendering, now suggests flawlessness. 'Complete' also answers the young man's question directly: he asked what he still lacks.

verse.text: But when the young man heard this saying, he went away grieving, for he had many possessions.
Then Jesus said to his disciples, “Truly I tell you, it is hard for a rich person to enter the kingdom of the heavens.

text.q: Again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.”

verse.note: The saying is deliberate exaggeration: the largest animal familiar in the region set against the smallest opening. The popular explanation that 'the Needle's Eye' was a small gate in Jerusalem has no ancient evidence behind it. The disciples' astonishment and Jesus' word 'impossible' in verse 26 show that a literal needle is meant.

verse.text: When the disciples heard this, they were greatly astonished and said, “Who then can be saved?”
Jesus looked at them and said, “With people this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.”
Then Peter said to him in reply, “Look, we have left everything and followed you. What then will there be for us?”

Jesus said to them, “Truly I tell you, at the renewal of all things, when the Son of Man sits on his glorious throne, you who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
verse.note: The single Greek word means 'rebirth' or 'renewal'. Greek and Jewish writers of the period used it for the restoration of the world or of a nation after catastrophe. Here it refers to the new order of the age to come, when God sets the world right; 'of all things' is supplied to make that cosmic sense clear, as most modern translations do.

text.q: And everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or wife or children or fields for the sake of my name will receive a hundred times as much and will inherit eternal life.

verse.note: Some early manuscripts lack 'or wife', and several modern critical editions omit the words as a copyist's addition drawn from Luke 18:29. The SBLGNT includes them and is followed here.

text.q: But many who are first will be last, and the last first.”
“For the kingdom of the heavens is like a landowner who went out at daybreak to hire workers for his vineyard.

verse.note: The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase characteristic of Matthew, and it is kept here. Most English translations flatten it to the singular 'heaven'. The meaning is the same.

text.q: After agreeing with the workers on a denarius for the day, he sent them into his vineyard.

verse.note: The denarius was a Roman silver coin. It is usually taken to be an ordinary day's pay for a labourer, and this parable is itself part of the evidence for that. The first workers are therefore offered a normal, fair wage.

text.q: Going out about the third hour, he saw others standing in the marketplace without work,

note.traditional: the third hour; about nine in the morning

verse.note: Daylight was divided into twelve hours counted from sunrise. The third hour is about nine in the morning, the sixth about noon, the ninth about three in the afternoon, and the eleventh about five, roughly an hour before the working day ended.

The Greek word means 'not working' and can describe either laziness or simple lack of employment. 'Idle' now suggests the former, but verse 7 shows these men are unhired, not unwilling, so 'without work' is used here and in verse 6.

text.q: and to them he said, ‘You go into the vineyard too, and I will give you whatever is just.’

verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two (right/righteous and just/justice). 'Just' is used here so that the reader can hear the echo in verse 13, where 'I am doing you no injustice' uses the same root. Most translations have 'whatever is right' here and 'I am doing you no wrong' there.

text.q: And they went. Going out again about the sixth hour and the ninth hour, he did the same.
About the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing there, and he said to them, ‘Why have you been standing here all day without work?’
They said to him, ‘Because no one has hired us.’ He said to them, ‘You go into the vineyard too.’
When evening came, the owner of the vineyard said to his foreman, ‘Call the workers and pay them their wages, beginning with the last and ending with the first.’
Those hired about the eleventh hour came and received a denarius each.
When the first came, they supposed they would receive more; but they too received a denarius each.
On receiving it they began to grumble against the landowner,
saying, ‘These last worked one hour, and you have made them equal to us, who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat.’
But he answered one of them, ‘Friend, I am doing you no injustice. Did you not agree with me on a denarius?
Take what is yours and go. I want to give this last one the same as I give you.
Am I not allowed to do what I want with what is mine? Or is your eye evil because I am good?’

note.term: is your eye evil because I am good
note.traditional: Is thine eye evil, because I am good? (KJV); are you envious because I am generous? (most modern versions)

verse.note: An 'evil eye' was a familiar Jewish idiom for a grudging, envious or stingy attitude (compare Deuteronomy 15:9 and Matthew 6:23), not a curse or a hostile stare. 'Good' here carries the sense of generous. The idiom is kept because it sets 'evil' against 'good', a contrast modern paraphrases lose.

text.q: So the last will be first, and the first last.”

note.term: So the last will be first, and the first last.
note.traditional: So the last shall be first, and the first last: for many be called, but few chosen. (KJV)

verse.note: Many later manuscripts add 'for many are called, but few are chosen' at the end of this verse, and the words appear in the King James Version. The earliest witnesses lack them. They are generally judged to have been carried over from Matthew 22:14, and the SBLGNT text translated here omits them.

verse.text: As Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took the twelve disciples aside by themselves, and on the way he said to them,

text.q: “Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death
and hand him over to the Gentiles to be mocked and flogged and crucified, and on the third day he will be raised.”

verse.note: One Greek word means both 'nations' and, in the plural from a Jewish standpoint, the non-Jewish peoples. Here it points to the Roman authorities, who carried out crucifixion. The same word is behind 'the rulers of the Gentiles' in verse 25, which could equally be heard as 'the rulers of the nations'.

verse.text: Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came to him with her sons, bowing down before him and asking something of him.
He said to her, “What do you want?” She said to him, “Say that these two sons of mine are to sit, one at your right and one at your left, in your kingdom.”
But Jesus answered, “You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I am about to drink?” They said to him, “We are able.”

note.term: You do not know what you are asking
note.traditional: You do not know what you are asking

verse.note: The Greek 'you' is plural here and in what follows. Although the mother made the request, Jesus answers the two brothers directly, and it is they who reply, 'We are able.'

In the Jewish Scriptures a cup that one is given to drink is a common image for the lot God assigns to a person, and very often for suffering or judgment. Jesus uses the same image of his death in Matthew 26:39.

verse.text: He said to them, “You will indeed drink my cup, but to sit at my right and at my left is not mine to give; it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.”
When the ten heard this, they were indignant at the two brothers.
But Jesus called them to him and said, “You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and the great ones wield authority over them.

text.q: It will not be so among you. Instead, whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant,
and whoever wants to be first among you must be your slave,
