just as the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”

verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for the price paid to free a slave or release a captive. The preposition translated 'for' has the sense 'in place of' or 'in exchange for'. 'Many' is a Semitic way of contrasting the one with the large number who benefit and need not imply that some are excluded. Many scholars hear an echo of Isaiah 53, though this is debated.

verse.text: As they were leaving Jericho, a large crowd followed him.
And there were two blind men sitting beside the road. When they heard that Jesus was passing by, they cried out, “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!”
verse.note: 'Son of David' was a title for the expected king from David's line, the Messiah. The blind men are therefore making a claim about who Jesus is, not merely naming his ancestry. This comes just before his entry into Jerusalem, where the crowds take up the same title.

verse.text: The crowd rebuked them, telling them to be quiet, but they cried out all the louder, “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!”
Jesus stopped, called them, and said, “What do you want me to do for you?”
They said to him, “Lord, that our eyes may be opened.”
Moved with compassion, Jesus touched their eyes, and immediately they could see again, and they followed him.
When they drew near to Jerusalem and came to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives, Jesus then sent two disciples,
saying to them, “Go into the village ahead of you, and at once you will find a donkey tied up, and a colt with her. Untie them and bring them to me.

text.q: And if anyone says anything to you, you are to say, ‘The Lord needs them,’ and he will send them at once.”

verse.note: The Greek can also be read 'Their master needs them', since 'of them' can attach either to 'lord' or to 'need', and the word for 'Lord' is also the ordinary word for an owner or master. Most translations take it as the text does, with Jesus referring to himself. A minority of interpreters take 'the Lord' to mean God, or the animals' owner.

verse.text: This happened so that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled:

text.q: “Say to daughter Zion, ‘Look, your king is coming to you, gentle and mounted on a donkey, and on a colt, the foal of a beast of burden.’”

verse.note: The traditional 'meek' now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes someone unassuming and not self-assertive, here a king who arrives without the trappings of war. 'Gentle' or 'humble' is the usual rendering in modern translations.

note.term: on a donkey, and on a colt

verse.note: The quotation joins an opening line from Isaiah 62:11 to Zechariah 9:9. In the Hebrew poetry of Zechariah the second line restates the first, so one animal is described twice. Matthew, alone among the Gospels, mentions both a donkey and her colt in the narrative. Whether he read the prophecy as naming two animals, or simply reports that the mother accompanied the colt, is debated.

verse.text: The disciples went and did as Jesus had directed them;
they brought the donkey and the colt and laid their cloaks on them, and he sat on them.
verse.note: The nearest antecedent of 'them' is the cloaks, and most interpreters understand that Jesus sat on the cloaks laid over the animal he rode. The Greek could also mean that he sat on the animals. The English is left as open as the Greek.

verse.text: Most of the crowd spread their own cloaks on the road, while others were cutting branches from the trees and spreading them on the road.
The crowds going ahead of him and those following were shouting, “Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!”
verse.note: A Hebrew expression transliterated into Greek, originally a plea meaning 'Save, please!' as in Psalm 118:25, the psalm from which the next line of the shout is taken. By the first century it appears to have become a shout of acclamation, which is how it works here with 'to the Son of David'. 'In the highest' means in the highest places, that is, in heaven.

verse.text: When he entered Jerusalem, the whole city was shaken, asking, “Who is this?”
And the crowds were saying, “This is the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth in Galilee.”
Jesus entered the temple and drove out all who were selling and buying in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves.
He said to them, “It is written, ‘My house will be called a house of prayer,’ but you are making it a den of bandits.”

note.traditional: a den of thieves; a den of robbers

verse.note: The Greek word denotes a brigand who robs with violence, as distinct from a thief who steals by stealth; it is the word later used of the two men crucified with Jesus. The phrase comes from Jeremiah 7:11, where the temple is pictured as the hideout to which wrongdoers retreat in safety, not as the place where the robbing is done. 'Robbers' remains the commonest modern rendering.

verse.text: Blind and lame people came to him in the temple, and he healed them.
But when the chief priests and the scribes saw the wonders he did, and the children shouting in the temple, “Hosanna to the Son of David!” they were indignant
and said to him, “Do you hear what these are saying?” Jesus said to them, “Yes. Have you never read, ‘Out of the mouths of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise for yourself’?”
And leaving them, he went out of the city to Bethany and spent the night there.
Early in the morning, as he was returning to the city, he was hungry.
Seeing a lone fig tree by the road, he went up to it and found nothing on it but leaves. He said to it, “May no fruit ever come from you again!” And the fig tree withered at once.
When the disciples saw it, they were amazed and said, “How did the fig tree wither at once?”

Jesus answered them, “Truly I tell you, if you have faith and do not doubt, not only will you do what was done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and thrown into the sea,’ it will happen.

text.q: And everything you ask for in prayer, believing, you will receive.”

verse.text: When he had come into the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came up to him as he was teaching and said, “By what authority are you doing these things? And who gave you this authority?”
Jesus answered them, “I too will ask you one question, and if you answer me, I too will tell you by what authority I am doing these things.
Where was John’s baptism from? From heaven, or from people?” They discussed it among themselves, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say to us, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’

text.q: But if we say, ‘From people,’ we are afraid of the crowd, for they all hold John to be a prophet.”

verse.text: So they answered Jesus, “We do not know.” He in turn said to them, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things.

text.q: “What do you think? A man had two sons. He went to the first and said, ‘Son, go and work in the vineyard today.’
He answered, ‘I will not,’ but afterward he changed his mind and went.

verse.note: The manuscripts give this parable in different forms. In the form followed here, the first son refuses and then goes. In another well-attested form the order is reversed, so that the son who obeys is the second and the answer in verse 31 is 'the last'. A third form has the hearers approve the son who said yes and did nothing; the point of the parable is the same in the first two forms.

text.q: He went to the second and said the same. He answered, ‘I will, sir,’ and did not go.

verse.text: Which of the two did the father’s will?” They said, “The first.” Jesus said to them, “Truly I tell you, the tax collectors and the prostitutes are going into the kingdom of God ahead of you.

text.q: For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and the prostitutes believed him. And you, when you saw this, did not even change your minds afterward and believe him.

verse.note: The phrase may mean that John himself lived rightly, or that he came teaching the right way of life that God requires; both fit Matthew's use of the word. Greek has one word-family where English has two (righteous and just, righteousness and justice), so 'the way of justice' would be an equally literal rendering.

text.q: “Listen to another parable. There was a landowner who planted a vineyard, put a fence around it, dug a winepress in it, and built a tower. Then he leased it to tenants and went abroad.

verse.note: The details of the vineyard, with its fence, winepress and tower, echo the song of the vineyard in Isaiah 5:1–7, where the vineyard is Israel and its owner is God. Hearers who knew that passage would have recognised the story as being about God and his people before any explanation was given.

text.q: When the season of fruits drew near, he sent his slaves to the tenants to collect his fruits.

verse.note: The Greek word means a slave, a person owned by a master, not a hired employee; landowners commonly used slaves as their agents. Several recent translations render 'slaves', while others retain 'servants' because of the associations slavery has for modern readers.

text.q: And the tenants seized his slaves; one they beat, another they killed, another they stoned.
Again he sent other slaves, more than the first, and they did the same to them.
Finally he sent his son to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’
But when the tenants saw the son, they said among themselves, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance.’
And they seized him, threw him out of the vineyard, and killed him.
So when the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants?”

verse.text: They said to him, “He will bring those wretches to a wretched end and lease the vineyard to other tenants, who will give him the fruits in their seasons.”
Jesus said to them, “Have you never read in the Scriptures, ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. This came from the Lord, and it is wonderful in our eyes’?

note.traditional: the head of the corner; the cornerstone

verse.note: Literally 'head of the corner', quoting Psalm 118:22–23. It may be a foundation stone at the corner of a building or the capstone that completes a wall or arch; scholars are divided. Either way it is the stone on which the structure depends.

text.q: For this reason I tell you that the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation that produces its fruits.

verse.note: The Greek word is the one that in the plural is usually rendered 'Gentiles'; in the singular, as here, it means a people or nation. The saying therefore does not simply say 'given to the Gentiles'. Who this 'nation' is has been much debated; many interpreters take it to be the community of Jesus's followers, Jewish and Gentile, in contrast to the leaders addressed in verse 45.

text.q: And anyone who falls on this stone will be shattered, and anyone it falls on, it will crush.”

verse.note: This verse is absent from a small number of early witnesses, and some editors bracket it as a possible borrowing from Luke 20:18. The great majority of manuscripts, including early ones, contain it, and the edition translated here prints it without brackets.

verse.text: When the chief priests and the Pharisees heard his parables, they realized that he was speaking about them.
They wanted to arrest him, but they feared the crowds, since they held him to be a prophet.
Jesus responded by speaking to them again in parables:

text.q: “The kingdom of the heavens is like a king who gave a wedding feast for his son.

verse.note: The Greek is plural, reflecting a Semitic way of speaking about God's dwelling that a first-century hearer would have noticed. Most English translations flatten it to 'heaven'. The plural is kept here because it is Matthew's characteristic phrase.

text.q: He sent his slaves to summon those who had been invited to the wedding feast, but they would not come.

verse.note: The Greek word denotes a person owned by a master, not a hired employee, and 'servants' softens that for a modern reader. Many recent translations now use 'slaves'. The attendants in verse 13 are a different Greek word and are rendered 'servants'.

text.q: Again he sent other slaves, saying, ‘Tell those who have been invited: “Look, I have prepared my dinner; my bulls and fattened cattle have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding feast.”’
But they paid no attention and went off, one to his own field, another to his business,
while the rest seized his slaves, abused them, and killed them.
The king was furious. He sent his troops, destroyed those murderers, and burned their city.
Then he said to his slaves, ‘The wedding feast is ready, but those who were invited were not worthy.
So go to where the roads lead out of the city, and invite to the wedding feast everyone you find.’
And those slaves went out into the roads and gathered everyone they found, both bad and good, and the wedding feast was filled with guests.
But when the king came in to look at the guests, he saw there a man who was not dressed in wedding clothes,
and he said to him, ‘Friend, how did you get in here without wedding clothes?’ But the man was struck silent.

verse.note: This is not the ordinary word for a friend but a polite form of address to someone whose name is not used, something like 'my good man'. In Matthew it is used only three times, each time to a person who is in the wrong (also 20:13 and 26:50), so it carries a note of reproach, not warmth.

text.q: Then the king said to the servants, ‘Bind him hand and foot and throw him out into the darkness outside. There, there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’
For many are invited, but few are chosen.”

verse.note: The traditional rendering is 'many are called'. The Greek word is from the same verb used throughout the parable for inviting guests to the feast, and 'invited' keeps that link audible. Some modern translations do the same. Others keep 'called' because of its use elsewhere in the New Testament for God's summons.

verse.text: Then the Pharisees went and made a plan to trap him in what he said.

They sent their disciples to him, together with the Herodians, saying, “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth, and that you defer to no one, for you show no partiality.
verse.note: These were evidently supporters of the family of Herod, which ruled by Rome's favor, though little else is known of them. They would have been expected to approve of paying Roman tax, while many Pharisees resented it. An answer either way could therefore be used against Jesus.

text.q: So tell us what you think: is it permitted to pay the poll tax to Caesar, or not?”

verse.note: The Greek borrows the Latin word census. It refers to the head tax Rome levied on subject peoples on the basis of a census, not to taxes in general. It was a sore point in Judea, where its introduction had provoked a revolt, so the question was politically dangerous.

verse.text: But Jesus, aware of their malice, said, “Why are you testing me, you hypocrites?
Show me the coin for the poll tax.” And they brought him a denarius.
verse.note: A denarius was a Roman silver coin, roughly a day's wage for a laborer. It carried the emperor's portrait and an inscription giving his titles, which on the common coin of the period included a claim to be son of the deified Augustus. Jesus's question in the next verse turns on that image and wording.

verse.text: He said to them, “Whose image is this, and whose inscription?”
They said to him, “Caesar’s.” Then he said to them, “So give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.”
verse.note: The questioners asked whether it was permitted to 'give' the tax. Jesus answers with a different, compound verb that normally means to pay what is owed or return what belongs to another. 'Give back' keeps that shift. 'Render' in older versions carried the same sense but is no longer heard that way.

verse.text: When they heard this they were amazed, and they left him and went away.
On that day Sadducees came to him, saying that there is no resurrection, and they asked him a question:

note.term: saying that there is no resurrection
note.traditional: who say there is no resurrection

verse.note: In the text translated here the phrase has no article, so it most naturally means that the Sadducees came asserting this. Many manuscripts add the article, giving 'Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection', a description of the group. Either way the point is the same: the Sadducees denied a resurrection, and their question is meant to make the idea look absurd.

text.q: “Teacher, Moses said, ‘If a man dies without having children, his brother shall marry his widow and raise up offspring for his brother.’

verse.note: The Sadducees summarize the law of levirate marriage in Deuteronomy 25:5–6. Under it a dead man's brother married the widow, and the first son counted as the dead man's heir. The Greek verb is a technical term for marrying as a brother-in-law. The verb for 'raise up' offspring is from the same root as the word for 'resurrection'.

text.q: Now there were seven brothers among us. The first married and died, and having no offspring he left his wife to his brother.
The same happened with the second and the third, down to the seventh.
Last of all, the woman died.
In the resurrection, then, which of the seven will she be the wife of? For they all had her.”

verse.text: Jesus answered them, “You are mistaken, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God.

text.q: For in the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels of God in heaven.

note.traditional: angels in heaven; the angels of God in heaven

verse.note: The Greek edition translated here reads 'angels of God'. Some important early manuscripts lack 'of God', and several modern editions and translations follow them. The meaning is not materially affected.

text.q: And as for the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was said to you by God:
‘I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob’? He is not the God of the dead but of the living.”

verse.text: And when the crowds heard this, they were astonished at his teaching.
When the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together,
and one of them, an expert in the Law, asked him a question to test him:
verse.note: The traditional 'lawyer' suggests a courtroom advocate. The word refers to a specialist in interpreting the Law of Moses, much the same as the 'scribes' elsewhere in the Gospels. Many modern translations render it this way. A few manuscripts omit the word in this verse.

text.q: “Teacher, which commandment in the Law is the greatest?”

verse.text: He said to him, “‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind.’

text.q: This is the greatest and first commandment.
A second is like it: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’
On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets.”

verse.text: While the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them a question:
“What do you think about the Messiah? Whose son is he?” They said to him, “David’s.”
verse.note: The Greek word is the one traditionally rendered 'Christ'. Here it has the article and is a title under discussion, the anointed king Israel expected, not a name for Jesus. 'Messiah' conveys what a first-century Jewish hearer would have heard. Several modern translations make the same distinction in the Gospels.

verse.text: He said to them, “How is it, then, that David, in the Spirit, calls him Lord, saying,

text.q: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand until I put your enemies under your feet”’?

note.term: The Lord said to my Lord
note.traditional: The LORD said unto my Lord

verse.note: This quotes Psalm 110:1. In the Hebrew the first 'Lord' is the divine name and the second is an ordinary word for a master or superior, but the Greek uses the same word for both. Jesus's argument assumes, as his hearers did, that David composed the psalm and that the second 'Lord' is the Messiah.

text.q: If David, then, calls him Lord, how is he his son?”

verse.text: And no one was able to answer him a word, nor from that day did anyone dare to ask him anything more.
Then Jesus spoke to the crowds and to his disciples,
saying, “The scribes and the Pharisees have seated themselves on the seat of Moses.
verse.note: The phrase stands for the authority to teach and apply the Law given through Moses. Stone seats of honor have been found in some ancient synagogues, and it is debated whether the expression refers to such a seat or is simply a figure of speech.

text.q: So do and keep everything they tell you, but do not do according to their deeds, for they say and do not do.
They tie up heavy loads and lay them on people’s shoulders, but they themselves are not willing to move them with a finger.
They do all their deeds to be seen by people: they make their phylacteries broad and their tassels long,

verse.note: These are the small leather cases containing passages of Scripture that Jewish men strapped to the forehead and arm at prayer (tefillin), following Deuteronomy 6:8. The tassels are those the Law required on the corners of a garment (Numbers 15:38). The criticism is of enlarging both for show, not of wearing them.

text.q: they love the place of honor at dinners and the front seats in the synagogues,
and the greetings in the marketplaces, and being called ‘Rabbi’ by people.
But you are not to be called ‘Rabbi,’ for one is your teacher, and you are all brothers.
And do not call anyone on earth your father, for one is your Father, the heavenly one.
Nor are you to be called instructors, because your instructor is one, the Messiah.

verse.note: The word occurs in the New Testament only in this verse. In everyday Greek of the period it commonly meant a teacher or private tutor, so 'instructors' is used here; older versions have 'masters' and some modern ones 'leaders'. It is distinct from the word translated 'teacher' in verse 8.

The Greek word is the one traditionally rendered 'Christ'. Here it has the article and functions as a title, the anointed king Israel expected, which 'Messiah' conveys to a modern reader. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels.

text.q: The greatest among you will be your servant.
Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.

But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you shut the kingdom of the heavens in people’s faces. For you do not go in yourselves, and those who are going in you do not allow to enter.

verse.note: The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase characteristic of Matthew. Most translations flatten it to 'heaven'; the plural is kept here because a first-century hearer would have heard it.

text.q: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you cross sea and dry land to make one convert, and when he becomes one, you make him twice as much a son of Gehenna as you are.

note.term: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites

verse.note: The numbering passes from verse 13 to verse 15. Verse 14 in older English Bibles (a woe about devouring widows' houses and making long prayers for show) is absent from the earliest manuscripts of Matthew and is generally thought to have been added from the similar saying in Mark 12:40 and Luke 20:47. The edition translated here does not include it.

Gehenna is a place name, the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, which had become the image for the place of final judgment. Many translations render it 'hell', usually with a footnote; the name is kept here so that it is not merged with Hades or later imagery. 'Son of' is a Semitic idiom for one who belongs to or is destined for something.

text.q: Woe to you, blind guides, who say, ‘Whoever swears by the sanctuary, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the sanctuary is bound.’

verse.note: Greek has two words that English Bibles usually both translate 'temple': one for the whole complex with its courts, and this one, which normally means the sanctuary building itself. The distinction matters in verse 35, where the altar stood in the court outside the sanctuary. Most translations use 'temple' here.

text.q: Blind fools! Which is greater, the gold or the sanctuary that made the gold holy?
And, ‘Whoever swears by the altar, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gift on it is bound.’
You blind men! Which is greater, the gift or the altar that makes the gift holy?
So whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it.
And whoever swears by the sanctuary swears by it and by the one who dwells in it.
And whoever swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by the one who sits on it.

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others.

verse.note: The Greek word covers both 'faith' and 'faithfulness'. Set alongside justice and mercy as a duty the Law requires, it here means the quality of being reliable and loyal, and most modern translations render it this way; older versions have 'faith'. The three terms echo prophetic summaries such as Micah 6:8.

text.q: Blind guides, who strain out the gnat but swallow the camel!

note.term: strain out the gnat but swallow the camel

verse.note: Wine was strained through cloth so as not to swallow a small insect, which the Law counted unclean. The camel was also an unclean animal and the largest one commonly seen. It is often suggested that the saying played on the similar-sounding Aramaic words for 'gnat' and 'camel'.

text.q: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you clean the outside of the cup and the dish, but inside they are full of plunder and self-indulgence.
Blind Pharisee! First clean the inside of the cup and the dish, so that the outside too may become clean.

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you are like whitewashed tombs, which on the outside appear beautiful but inside are full of the bones of the dead and every kind of uncleanness.
So you too on the outside appear righteous to people, but inside you are full of hypocrisy and lawlessness.
Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you build the tombs of the prophets and decorate the monuments of the righteous,
and you say, ‘If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partners with them in the blood of the prophets.’
So you testify against yourselves that you are sons of those who murdered the prophets.
You, then, fill up the measure of your fathers!
Snakes, offspring of vipers! How are you to escape the judgment of Gehenna?
For this reason, look, I am sending you prophets and wise men and scribes. Some of them you will kill and crucify, and some of them you will flog in your synagogues and pursue from town to town,

so that upon you may come all the righteous blood shed on the earth, from the blood of Abel the righteous to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar.

verse.note: The murder described matches that of Zechariah son of Jehoiada, stoned in the temple court in 2 Chronicles 24:20–22, whereas 'son of Barachiah' is the designation of the prophet Zechariah (Zechariah 1:1). How the two are related is disputed. Since Chronicles stands last in the traditional Hebrew ordering of the Scriptures, 'Abel to Zechariah' probably means from the first murder in Scripture to the last.

text.q: Truly I tell you, all these things will come upon this generation.
Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her! How often I wanted to gather your children, the way a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you did not want it!
Look, your house is left to you desolate.

verse.note: The 'house' may be the temple, the city of Jerusalem, or the people as a household; the temple is the most common interpretation, given what follows in the next chapter, but the others are possible. A few early manuscripts lack the word 'desolate'.

text.q: For I tell you, from now on you will not see me until you say, ‘Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord.’”

verse.text: Jesus left the temple and was going on his way when his disciples came up to point out to him the temple buildings.
But he answered them, “Do you not see all these things? Truly I tell you, not one stone will be left here on another that will not be thrown down.”
As he was sitting on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to him privately and said, “Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign of your coming and of the close of the age?”
verse.note: The Greek word means both arrival and presence, and was the regular term for the official visit of a king or emperor to a city. Matthew is the only Gospel to use it, four times in this chapter (verses 3, 27, 37, 39). 'Coming' is the standard rendering and is kept here.

verse.text: Jesus answered them, “Watch out that no one leads you astray.

text.q: For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am the Messiah,’ and they will lead many astray.

verse.note: The Greek word translates the Hebrew for 'anointed one', the king Israel expected. Here it is a title that pretenders claim for themselves, not a name, so 'Messiah' is used, as it is in verse 23 and in 'false messiahs' in verse 24. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels and keep 'Christ' where the word functions as a name.

text.q: You are going to hear of wars and rumors of wars. See that you are not alarmed, for this must happen, but it is not yet the end.
For nation will rise up against nation and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be famines and earthquakes in various places.

verse.note: The same Greek word, in the plural, is rendered 'Gentiles' elsewhere in this translation when it means the non-Jewish peoples. Here and in verses 9 and 14 the peoples of the world as political and ethnic units are in view, so 'nation' and 'nations' are used. Dividing the word by sense in this way is standard practice.

text.q: But all these are the beginning of the birth pains.
Then they will hand you over to suffering and will kill you, and you will be hated by all the nations because of my name.

verse.note: The word means pressure, and so distress or oppression of any kind; it was an ordinary word, not a technical term. The traditional 'tribulation' has become a label for a specific end-time period, which says more than the Greek does. The same word is used in verses 21 ('great suffering') and 29.

text.q: And then many will fall away, and they will hand one another over and hate one another.
And many false prophets will rise up and lead many astray.
And because lawlessness will increase, the love of most will grow cold.
But the one who endures to the end will be saved.
And this good news of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole inhabited world as a testimony to all the nations, and then the end will come.

verse.note: The word meant an announcement of good news, such as a victory or a ruler's accession, and the related verb is used in the Greek version of Isaiah for announcing God's reign. 'Gospel' is the traditional rendering and many translations keep it; others use 'good news', as here, because 'gospel' now sounds like a purely religious term.

text.q: So when you see the abomination of desolation, spoken of through the prophet Daniel, standing in the holy place—let the reader understand—

verse.note: The phrase comes from Daniel (9:27, 11:31, 12:11), where it describes something detestable that defiles the sanctuary and leaves it desolate. Jewish readers connected it with the pagan altar set up in the Jerusalem temple under Antiochus IV in 167 BC; 1 Maccabees 1:54 uses the same phrase for it. Jesus points to a further event of that kind. Which event is disputed, though many connect it with the Roman war of AD 66–70.

These words may be part of Jesus's speech, addressed to the reader of Daniel, or an aside by the evangelist to the person reading the Gospel aloud. The same words appear in Mark 13:14, where Daniel is not named, and many scholars take them as an editorial aside. The text here leaves them inside the speech.

text.q: then those in Judea must flee to the mountains;
the one on the housetop must not go down to take what is in his house,
and the one in the field must not turn back to get his cloak.
But woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing in those days!
Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on a Sabbath.
For then there will be great suffering, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, and never will be.
And if those days had not been cut short, no one would be saved; but for the sake of the chosen ones those days will be cut short.

verse.note: The Greek is the ordinary word for someone or something chosen or picked out, and in the Septuagint it is used of Israel as God's chosen people. 'The elect' is the traditional rendering and means the same thing, but it now sounds like a technical theological term. Most major translations still use 'the elect'.

text.q: Then if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Messiah!’ or ‘Here!’—do not believe it.
For false messiahs and false prophets will rise up and will give great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the chosen ones.
See, I have told you beforehand.
So if they say to you, ‘Look, he is in the wilderness,’ do not go out; ‘Look, he is in the inner rooms,’ do not believe it.
For just as the lightning comes out of the east and is seen as far as the west, so will the coming of the Son of Man be.
Wherever the carcass is, there the vultures will gather.
Immediately after the suffering of those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from the sky, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken.

And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in the sky, and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory.
And he will send out his angels with a great trumpet blast, and they will gather his chosen ones from the four winds, from one end of the heavens to the other.
From the fig tree learn this parable: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out leaves, you know that summer is near.
So you also, when you see all these things, know that he is near, at the very door.

note.traditional: it is near / he is near

verse.note: The Greek verb has no expressed subject, so the phrase could equally be 'it is near', meaning the end or the events just described. Translations are divided. 'He' is chosen here because the preceding verses describe the coming of the Son of Man, and the image of someone standing at the door suits a person.

text.q: Truly I tell you, this generation will certainly not pass away until all these things have happened.

verse.note: Elsewhere in Matthew this phrase refers to Jesus's contemporaries, and that is its most natural sense here. Because the verse is hard to fit with a far-future reading of the chapter, some have proposed 'this race' or 'this kind of people', and others limit 'all these things' to the events leading up to the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70. The interpretation is disputed. The rendering itself is not seriously in doubt.

text.q: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away.
But about that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of the heavens, nor the Son, but the Father alone.

verse.note: Many later manuscripts lack these words in Matthew, while important early witnesses include them. They are undisputed in the parallel at Mark 13:32. Most editors think copyists dropped them because of the difficulty of the Son not knowing, and the SBLGNT prints them.

text.q: For as the days of Noah were, so will the coming of the Son of Man be.
For just as in those days before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, right up to the day Noah entered the ark,
and they knew nothing until the flood came and swept them all away, so too will the coming of the Son of Man be.
Then two men will be in the field: one is taken and one is left.
Two women will be grinding at the mill: one is taken and one is left.
So stay awake, because you do not know on what day your Lord is coming.
But know this: if the master of the house had known in which watch of the night the thief was coming, he would have stayed awake and would not have let his house be broken into.
For this reason you also must be ready, because the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect.
Who then is the faithful and sensible slave, whom his master has put in charge of his household to give them their food at the proper time?

verse.note: The Greek word denotes a person owned by a master, not a hired employee, and a first-century hearer would have understood it that way. The traditional 'servant' softens this. Slaves could hold positions of considerable responsibility, as this household manager does. Many recent translations also use 'slave'.

text.q: Blessed is that slave whom his master, when he comes, will find doing so.
Truly I tell you, he will put him in charge of all that he owns.
But if that bad slave says in his heart, ‘My master is a long time coming,’
and begins to beat his fellow slaves, and eats and drinks with the drunkards,
the master of that slave will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour that he does not know,
and will cut him in two and assign him his place with the hypocrites. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”
“Then the kingdom of the heavens will be like ten young women who took their torches and went out to meet the bridegroom.

verse.note: Matthew's Greek has the plural, 'the heavens', a Semitic turn of phrase that a first-century hearer would have noticed. Most English translations flatten it to 'heaven'; the plural is kept here.

The Greek word denotes a girl of marriageable age who is not yet married. Virginity is assumed but is not the point of the story, and the modern English word 'virgins' puts the stress there. 'Bridesmaids' is a reasonable inference from the scene but says more than the word does.

The Greek word ordinarily means a torch, and a different word is used for the small household oil lamp. Many commentators picture poles wrapped in oil-soaked rags, which burn quickly and need fresh oil, and that suits an outdoor night procession. The word can occasionally mean a lamp, however, and most English versions translate it so; the question is not settled.

text.q: Five of them were foolish and five were sensible.
For the foolish ones, when they took their torches, took no oil with them,
but the sensible ones took oil in flasks along with their torches.
As the bridegroom was a long time coming, they all grew drowsy and fell asleep.
But in the middle of the night there was a shout: ‘Look, the bridegroom! Come out to meet him!’
Then all those young women got up and put their torches in order.
The foolish ones said to the sensible, ‘Give us some of your oil, because our torches are going out.’
But the sensible ones answered, ‘No, there may well not be enough for us and for you. Go instead to those who sell it and buy some for yourselves.’
But while they were going off to buy it, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went in with him to the wedding feast, and the door was shut.
Later the rest of the young women came too, saying, ‘Sir, sir, open up for us!’

verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary respectful address to a superior and also the word for 'Lord'. It is the same word translated 'Master' in verse 20 and 'Lord' in verse 37. Within the story the young women are addressing the bridegroom, so 'Sir' is used. Matthew's readers would also have heard an echo of 7:21–23, where people cry 'Lord, Lord' and are told 'I never knew you.'

text.q: But he answered, ‘Truly I tell you, I do not know you.’
So keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.
“For it is like a man going abroad, who called his own slaves and handed his property over to them.

verse.note: The Greek word means a slave, a person owned by a master, not a hired servant. Slaves in the ancient world could be trusted with managing very large sums on their owner's behalf, as here. English versions are divided between 'servants' and 'slaves'.

text.q: To one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one, to each according to his own ability, and he went abroad. Immediately

verse.note: A talent was a large weight of silver or gold used as a unit of money, roughly six thousand days' wages for a labourer. Even the slave given one talent is therefore entrusted with a fortune. The English sense of 'talent' as a natural ability comes from this parable and is not what the word meant.

note.traditional: and straightway took his journey (KJV); modern versions mostly attach it to the first slave

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts have no punctuation, so 'immediately' can go either with the master's departure or with the first slave's getting to work. The SBLGNT and most modern translations take it with the slave, which this translation follows. The word falls at the end of verse 15 in the traditional numbering.

text.q: the one who had received the five talents went and put them to work and gained five more.
In the same way the one with the two gained two more.
But the one who had received the one went off, dug a hole in the ground, and hid his master’s money.
After a long time the master of those slaves came and settled accounts with them.
The one who had received the five talents came forward and brought five more talents, saying, ‘Master, you handed five talents over to me. See, I have gained five more talents.’
His master said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful slave! You were faithful over a few things; I will put you in charge of many. Enter into your master’s joy.’
The one with the two talents also came forward and said, ‘Master, you handed two talents over to me. See, I have gained two more talents.’
His master said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful slave! You were faithful over a few things; I will put you in charge of many. Enter into your master’s joy.’
Then the one who had received the one talent also came forward and said, ‘Master, I knew that you are a hard man, reaping where you did not sow and gathering from where you did not scatter.
So I was afraid, and I went off and hid your talent in the ground. See, you have what is yours.’
But his master answered him, ‘You wicked and lazy slave! You knew that I reap where I did not sow and gather from where I did not scatter?
Then you should have deposited my money with the bankers, and when I came I would have received back what is mine with interest.
So take the talent from him and give it to the one who has the ten talents.
For to everyone who has, more will be given, and he will have more than enough; but from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away.
And throw the useless slave out into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’
“When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him, then he will sit on his glorious throne.
All the nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate people from one another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats,

verse.note: One Greek word means both 'nations' and, in the plural, 'Gentiles', the non-Jewish peoples. Most interpreters take the phrase here to mean the whole of humanity, as in 24:14 and 28:19. A minority take it as the Gentile or non-Christian peoples, judged by how they treated Jesus's followers.

text.q: and he will place the sheep at his right and the goats at his left.
Then the king will say to those at his right, ‘Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.
For I was hungry and you gave me something to eat, I was thirsty and you gave me a drink, I was a stranger and you took me in,
naked and you clothed me, I was sick and you looked after me, I was in prison and you came to me.’

verse.note: The Greek verb means to go to see someone in order to help or care for them, not merely to pay a call. The same verb is used in verse 43 of both the sick and the prisoner. In the ancient world prisoners depended on outsiders for food and other necessities.

text.q: Then the righteous will answer him, ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you a drink?
When did we see you a stranger and take you in, or naked and clothe you?
When did we see you sick or in prison and come to you?’
And the king will answer them, ‘Truly I tell you, insofar as you did it for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did it for me.’

verse.note: The Greek plural regularly covers both sexes. Who is meant is disputed. Many readers take it as anyone in need. Many scholars note that elsewhere in Matthew Jesus's 'brothers' are his disciples (12:49–50; 28:10), and take it as his followers or messengers, as in 10:40–42. The translation leaves both readings open.

text.q: Then he will also say to those at his left, ‘Go away from me, you who are cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.

verse.note: The Greek adjective is formed from the word for 'age'. In Jewish usage it describes what belongs to the age to come, so it speaks of kind as well as length. 'Eternal' is the standard rendering and is kept here and in verse 46 for fire, punishment and life alike. A minority of translators prefer 'of the age to come'.

text.q: For I was hungry and you gave me nothing to eat, I was thirsty and you gave me no drink,
I was a stranger and you did not take me in, naked and you did not clothe me, sick and in prison and you did not look after me.’
Then they too will answer, ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty or a stranger or naked or sick or in prison and not serve you?’
Then he will answer them, ‘Truly I tell you, insofar as you did not do it for one of the least of these, you did not do it for me either.’
And these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.”

verse.text: When Jesus had finished all these words, he said to his disciples,

text.q: “You know that after two days the Passover comes, and the Son of Man is handed over to be crucified.”

verse.note: The Greek verb means to hand someone over into another's custody or power; Greek has a different word for 'betray'. Matthew uses this one verb for what Judas does, for what happens to the Son of Man, and later for what the authorities do to Jesus, and a single rendering keeps those links visible. Most translations use 'betray' where Judas is the subject and 'deliver' or 'hand over' elsewhere.

verse.text: Then the chief priests and the elders of the people gathered in the courtyard of the high priest, who was called Caiaphas,
and they plotted together to seize Jesus by deceit and kill him.
But they were saying, “Not during the festival, or there may be a riot among the people.”
Now when Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper,
a woman came to him with an alabaster jar of very costly perfumed oil, and she poured it over his head as he reclined at table.
When the disciples saw this, they were indignant and said, “Why this waste?

text.q: This could have been sold for a high price and given to the poor.”

verse.text: But Jesus, aware of this, said to them, “Why are you making trouble for the woman? She has done a good deed for me.

text.q: For you always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me.
When she poured this perfumed oil on my body, she did it to prepare me for burial.
Truly I tell you, wherever this good news is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will also be told, in memory of her.”

verse.note: The Greek word meant a welcome announcement, such as news of a victory, and a first-century hearer heard that ordinary sense. 'Gospel' once meant the same but now suggests a book or a body of doctrine. Many translations keep 'gospel' here; several modern ones use 'good news'.

verse.text: Then one of the Twelve, the one called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests
and said, “What are you willing to give me if I hand him over to you?” They weighed out thirty silver coins for him.

note.traditional: covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver

verse.note: The verb is literally 'set' or 'weighed', the old way of paying in silver, and the wording echoes the Greek version of Zechariah 11:12, where a shepherd's wages are weighed out as thirty pieces of silver. Thirty shekels of silver is also the compensation set in Exodus 21:32 for a slave killed by an ox. Some translations render 'counted out' or 'agreed to pay'.

verse.text: And from then on he was looking for an opportunity to hand him over.
On the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples came to Jesus and said, “Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?”
He said, “Go into the city to a certain man and say to him, ‘The Teacher says: My time is near; I am keeping the Passover at your house with my disciples.’”
The disciples did as Jesus had directed them, and they prepared the Passover.
When evening came, he was reclining at table with the twelve disciples,
and while they were eating he said, “Truly I tell you, one of you will hand me over.”
They were deeply grieved, and each one began to say to him, “Surely it is not I, Lord?”
He answered, “The one who has dipped his hand in the bowl with me, he will hand me over.

text.q: The Son of Man goes as it is written about him, but woe to that man through whom the Son of Man is handed over! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.”

verse.text: Judas, the one who was handing him over, answered, “Surely it is not I, Rabbi?” He said to him, “You have said it.”
verse.note: The reply is an indirect affirmation: it concedes the point while leaving the words in the questioner's mouth. Some read it as a plain 'Yes', others as more reserved ('That is your way of putting it'). Jesus gives the same answer to the high priest in verse 64, where what follows shows it is not a denial.

verse.text: While they were eating, Jesus took bread, and after saying the blessing he broke it, gave it to the disciples, and said, “Take, eat; this is my body.”
Then he took a cup, and after giving thanks he gave it to them, saying, “Drink from it, all of you,

text.q: for this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.

note.traditional: of the new testament; of the new covenant

verse.note: Many later manuscripts read 'the new covenant', the wording behind the King James Version. The earliest witnesses lack 'new', which was probably added from the parallel wording in Luke 22:20 and 1 Corinthians 11:25. The phrase 'blood of the covenant' recalls Exodus 24:8.

text.q: I tell you, from now on I will not drink of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom.”

verse.text: And after singing a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
Then Jesus said to them, “All of you will fall away because of me this night, for it is written, ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.’

text.q: But after I have been raised, I will go ahead of you to Galilee.”

verse.text: Peter answered him, “Even if all fall away because of you, I will never fall away.”
Jesus said to him, “Truly I tell you, this very night, before a rooster crows, you will deny me three times.”
Peter said to him, “Even if I must die with you, I will never deny you.” And all the disciples said the same.
Then Jesus came with them to a place called Gethsemane, and he said to the disciples, “Sit here while I go over there and pray.”
Taking with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be grieved and deeply troubled.
Then he said to them, “My soul is overwhelmed with grief, to the point of death. Remain here and stay awake with me.”
Going a little farther, he fell on his face, praying and saying, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me. Yet not as I will, but as you will.”
Then he came to the disciples and found them sleeping, and he said to Peter, “So none of you had the strength to stay awake with me for one hour?

text.q: Stay awake and pray, so that you do not enter into testing. The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.”

verse.note: The Greek noun covers both a trial that tests a person and an enticement to do wrong. Here the coming arrest is a test of the disciples' loyalty rather than a lure to sin, so 'testing' is used. 'Temptation' is the traditional rendering, and some modern translations have 'the time of trial'.

verse.text: Again, a second time, he went away and prayed, “My Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done.”
And when he came back he again found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy.
So he left them, went away again, and prayed a third time, saying the same words once more.
Then he came to the disciples and said to them, “Are you still sleeping and resting? Look, the hour has come near, and the Son of Man is being handed over into the hands of sinners.

note.term: Are you still sleeping and resting?
note.traditional: Sleep on now, and take your rest

verse.note: The Greek can be read as a question, as a command (perhaps ironic), or as an exclamation. The traditional rendering is the command, but it sits awkwardly with 'Get up, let us go' in the next verse, and many modern translations read a question, as here. The phrase rendered 'still' could also mean 'from now on' or 'for the time that remains'.

text.q: Get up, let us go. Look, the one handing me over has come near.”

verse.text: While he was still speaking, Judas, one of the Twelve, arrived, and with him a large crowd with swords and clubs, sent from the chief priests and elders of the people.
Now the one handing him over had given them a sign, saying, “The one I kiss is the man; seize him.”
He went straight up to Jesus and said, “Greetings, Rabbi!” and kissed him.
Jesus said to him, “Friend, do what you are here for.” Then they came forward, laid hands on Jesus, and seized him.

note.term: do what you are here for

verse.note: The Greek is a terse fragment, literally 'for what you are here'. It can be completed as a command, as here and in most modern translations, or as a question ('Why have you come?'), as in older versions. The word rendered 'Friend' is not the usual word for a friend but an address to a companion or associate; in Matthew's two other uses (20:13; 22:12) it addresses someone in the wrong.

verse.text: And one of those with Jesus reached out his hand, drew his sword, struck the high priest’s slave, and cut off his ear.
verse.note: The Greek word denotes a slave, a person owned by a master, not a hired servant. English Bibles have traditionally softened it to 'servant'; several recent translations use 'slave' or 'bondservant'. The 'slave girl' of verse 69 is likewise a female household slave in Greek.

verse.text: Then Jesus said to him, “Put your sword back in its place, for all who take up the sword will perish by the sword.

text.q: Or do you think that I cannot call on my Father, and he will at once put at my side more than twelve legions of angels?
How then would the scriptures be fulfilled, that it must happen this way?”

verse.text: At that hour Jesus said to the crowds, “Have you come out with swords and clubs to arrest me, as if against a bandit? Day after day I sat in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me.
verse.note: The Greek word means an armed robber or brigand, someone who uses violence, not a sneak thief; Josephus also uses it of armed insurgents. Older translations have 'thief' or 'robber', and some modern ones have 'bandit' or 'one leading a rebellion'. The same word describes the two men crucified with Jesus in the next chapter.

verse.text: But all this has happened so that the scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled.” Then all the disciples left him and fled.
Those who had seized Jesus led him away to Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and the elders had gathered.
Peter was following him at a distance, as far as the high priest’s courtyard, and going inside he sat with the attendants to see how it would end.
Now the chief priests and the whole council were looking for false testimony against Jesus so that they could put him to death,
but they found none, though many false witnesses came forward. At last two came forward
and said, “This man said, ‘I am able to destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days.’”
The high priest stood up and said to him, “Do you answer nothing? What is it that these men testify against you?”
But Jesus kept silent. And the high priest said to him, “I put you under oath by the living God: tell us whether you are the Messiah, the Son of God.”
verse.note: The Greek word is the one usually rendered 'Christ'. Here it is a title, the anointed king Israel expected, and the high priest is asking whether Jesus claims that office; 'Messiah' conveys the title where 'Christ' now reads as a name. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels.

verse.text: Jesus said to him, “You have said it. But I tell you, from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the Power and coming on the clouds of heaven.”
verse.note: 'The Power' is a reverent Jewish way of referring to God without naming him. The sentence combines Psalm 110:1 (seated at God's right hand) with Daniel 7:13 (one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven), and it is this claim that the high priest treats as blasphemy.

verse.text: Then the high priest tore his clothes and said, “He has blasphemed! What further need do we have of witnesses? Look, now you have heard the blasphemy.
What do you think?” They answered, “He deserves death.”
Then they spat in his face and struck him with their fists, and some slapped him,
saying, “Prophesy to us, Messiah! Who is it that hit you?”
Now Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard, and a slave girl came up to him and said, “You too were with Jesus the Galilean.”
But he denied it in front of them all, saying, “I do not know what you are talking about.”
When he had gone out to the gateway, another woman saw him and said to those who were there, “This man was with Jesus the Nazarene.”
And again he denied it, with an oath: “I do not know the man.”
After a little while the bystanders came up and said to Peter, “Surely you too are one of them, for the way you speak gives you away.”
Then he began to call down curses and to swear, “I do not know the man!” And immediately a rooster crowed.
verse.note: The Greek verb has no object. Most take it that Peter called down curses on himself if he was lying, to strengthen his oath; a minority view is that he cursed Jesus to prove he was no disciple. The rendering leaves the object unstated, as the Greek does.

verse.text: And Peter remembered the word Jesus had spoken: “Before a rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” And he went outside and wept bitterly.
When morning came, all the chief priests and the elders of the people reached a decision against Jesus, to put him to death.
They bound him, led him away, and handed him over to Pilate the governor.
Then Judas, who had handed him over, seeing that Jesus had been condemned, was seized with remorse and returned the thirty silver coins to the chief priests and elders,
verse.note: The Greek verb means to hand over or deliver up. It is the same word used when the priests hand Jesus to Pilate (v. 2) and when Pilate hands him over to be crucified (v. 26). Most translations switch to 'betray' when Judas is the subject, which is a fair description of the act but hides the chain of handings-over that runs through the narrative. Greek had a separate word for 'betray'.

verse.text: saying, “I have sinned by handing over innocent blood.” But they said, “What is that to us? See to it yourself.”
Throwing the silver coins into the sanctuary, he withdrew, and he went away and hanged himself.
verse.note: Greek has two words that are usually both translated 'temple': one for the whole complex with its courts, and this one, for the sanctuary building itself. Most translations do not distinguish them. How Judas could throw coins into a building only priests entered is unclear; Matthew may be using the word loosely or echoing Zechariah 11:13, where the silver is thrown into the house of the Lord.

verse.text: The chief priests took the silver coins and said, “It is not lawful to put them into the temple treasury, since they are the price of blood.”
So, having reached a decision, they used them to buy the Potter’s Field as a burial place for foreigners.
That is why that field has been called the Field of Blood to this day.
Then what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled: “And they took the thirty silver coins, the price of the one who was priced, whom some of the sons of Israel had priced,
verse.note: The words quoted are closest to Zechariah 11:12–13, not to any passage in Jeremiah. The usual explanation is that Matthew combines Zechariah with Jeremiah's passages about a potter, innocent blood and the purchase of a field (Jeremiah 18–19 and 32) and names the better-known prophet. The question remains debated.

text.q: and they gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord directed me.”

verse.text: Now Jesus stood before the governor, and the governor questioned him, saying, “Are you the king of the Jews?” Jesus said, “You say so.”
verse.note: Literally 'You are saying it.' The reply neither denies the title nor plainly claims it. It can be heard as a guarded yes ('it is as you say') or as putting the words back on Pilate ('that is your way of putting it'). Most interpreters take it as a qualified affirmation; the translation leaves it as open as the Greek.

verse.text: And while he was being accused by the chief priests and elders, he gave no answer.
Then Pilate said to him, “Do you not hear how many things they are testifying against you?”
But he gave him no answer, not even to a single charge, so that the governor was greatly amazed.
Now at the festival the governor was accustomed to release one prisoner to the crowd, whichever one they wanted.
At that time they had a notorious prisoner called Jesus Barabbas.
verse.note: Most manuscripts read simply 'Barabbas' here and in verse 17. The Greek edition translated here prints 'Jesus Barabbas' in both places, a reading found in a small number of witnesses and known to Origen in the third century. Many scholars think copyists dropped the name 'Jesus' out of reverence, but the matter is not settled, and some editions mark the name as doubtful.

verse.text: So when they had gathered, Pilate said to them, “Whom do you want me to release to you: Jesus Barabbas, or Jesus who is called the Messiah?”
verse.note: Pilate is referring to a title, the anointed king Israel expected, not to a surname. 'Messiah' lets a modern reader hear that. This translation keeps 'Christ' where the word works as part of Jesus's name, and several modern translations make the same distinction.

verse.text: For he knew that it was out of envy that they had handed him over.
While he was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent word to him: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for I have suffered much today in a dream because of him.”
But the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowds to ask for Barabbas and to have Jesus destroyed.
The governor asked them, “Which of the two do you want me to release to you?” They said, “Barabbas.”
Pilate said to them, “Then what shall I do with Jesus who is called the Messiah?” They all said, “Let him be crucified!”
He said, “Why, what evil has he done?” But they shouted all the more, “Let him be crucified!”

When Pilate saw that he was getting nowhere, and that instead a riot was starting, he took water and washed his hands in front of the crowd, saying, “I am innocent of this man’s blood. See to it yourselves.”
And all the people answered, “His blood be on us and on our children!”

note.term: His blood be on us and on our children!

verse.note: The wording is a biblical formula for accepting responsibility for a death (compare 2 Samuel 1:16). Many interpreters think Matthew has in view the generation that lived to see Jerusalem destroyed in AD 70. The verse was later used to blame Jews of every age for the death of Jesus, a use that goes well beyond what the narrative says.

verse.text: Then he released Barabbas to them; and after having Jesus flogged, he handed him over to be crucified.
Then the governor’s soldiers took Jesus into the headquarters and gathered the whole cohort around him.
They stripped him and put a scarlet cloak on him,
and after twisting together a crown of thorns they put it on his head and put a reed in his right hand. Kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying, “Hail, king of the Jews!”
And they spat on him, took the reed, and kept striking him on the head.
When they had mocked him, they stripped him of the cloak, put his own clothes on him, and led him away to crucify him.
As they were going out, they found a man of Cyrene named Simon; they pressed him into service to carry his cross.
And when they came to a place called Golgotha, which means Place of a Skull,
they gave him wine mixed with gall to drink; but when he had tasted it, he refused to drink.
When they had crucified him, they divided his clothes among themselves by casting lots,
and they sat down and kept watch over him there.
Above his head they put the charge against him in writing: “This is Jesus, the king of the Jews.”
Then two bandits were crucified with him, one on his right and one on his left.
verse.note: The word means someone who takes by violence, a brigand or bandit; Greek had a different word for a sneak thief. Josephus often uses it for armed rebels, and because crucifixion was a Roman penalty for sedition, some scholars think these men were insurrectionists. That is possible but not certain. Some modern translations also have 'bandits' or 'rebels'.

verse.text: Those passing by hurled abuse at him, shaking their heads
and saying, “You who would destroy the sanctuary and build it in three days, save yourself! If you are God’s Son, come down from the cross!”
In the same way the chief priests also, along with the scribes and elders, mocked him and said,

text.q: “He saved others; himself he cannot save. He is the king of Israel! Let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him.
He trusts in God; let God rescue him now, if he wants him. For he said, ‘I am God’s Son.’”

verse.text: And the bandits who were crucified with him also taunted him in the same way.
From the sixth hour darkness came over the whole land until the ninth hour.
verse.note: Hours were counted from sunrise, so the sixth hour is about noon and the ninth about three in the afternoon. The word translated 'land' can also mean 'earth'; most translations take it to mean the region.

verse.text: About the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?” that is, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

note.term: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?

verse.note: This is the opening line of Psalm 22, given first in Semitic words and then in Greek. The psalm is echoed several times in this chapter: the dividing of clothes by lot (v. 35), the shaking of heads (v. 39) and the taunt 'He trusts in God; let God rescue him' (v. 43). The bystanders' confusion with Elijah turns on the sound of 'Eli'.

verse.text: Some of those standing there, when they heard it, said, “This man is calling Elijah.”
At once one of them ran and took a sponge, filled it with sour wine, put it on a reed, and gave it to him to drink.
But the rest said, “Wait, let us see whether Elijah comes to save him.”
But Jesus cried out again with a loud voice and gave up his spirit.
And look, the curtain of the sanctuary was split in two from top to bottom, the earth shook, the rocks were split,
the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the holy ones who had fallen asleep were raised,
verse.note: 'Saints' now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek word means those set apart for God, and here it refers to the faithful dead. Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'holy people'.

verse.text: and coming out of the tombs after his resurrection they went into the holy city and appeared to many.
When the centurion and those with him who were keeping watch over Jesus saw the earthquake and the things that were happening, they were terrified and said, “Truly this man was God’s Son!”
verse.note: The Greek has no article and could be translated 'a son of a god', which is what a Roman soldier might naturally have meant. Greek does not need the article here to carry the definite sense, and Matthew uses the same article-less phrase in the taunt of verse 43, which the soldiers' words answer. Most translations have 'the Son of God'; 'God's Son' keeps the echo and something of the openness.

verse.text: Many women were there, watching from a distance; they had followed Jesus from Galilee, serving him.
Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee.
When evening came, there came a rich man from Arimathea named Joseph, who had himself also become a disciple of Jesus.
He went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then Pilate ordered it to be given to him.
Joseph took the body, wrapped it in a clean linen cloth,
and laid it in his own new tomb, which he had cut in the rock. Then he rolled a large stone against the entrance of the tomb and went away.
Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the tomb.
The next day, that is, the day after the Preparation, the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered before Pilate
verse.note: 'Preparation' was the ordinary Jewish name for the day before the Sabbath, that is, Friday. Matthew's roundabout phrase therefore means the Sabbath itself. Why he avoids naming it is uncertain.

verse.text: and said, “Sir, we remember that while he was still alive that deceiver said, ‘After three days I will be raised.’

text.q: So give orders for the tomb to be made secure until the third day; otherwise his disciples may come and steal him and tell the people, ‘He has been raised from the dead,’ and the last deception will be worse than the first.”

verse.text: Pilate said to them, “You have a guard. Go, make it as secure as you know how.”
verse.note: The Greek verb form can be a statement ('You have a guard') or a command ('Take a guard'). As a statement it may mean that Pilate is granting them soldiers, or that he is telling them to use their own temple police. The Latin loanword used for 'guard' and the soldiers' answerability to the governor in 28:14 suggest Roman troops, but the point is disputed.

verse.text: So they went and made the tomb secure with the guard, after sealing the stone.
After the Sabbath, as the first day of the week was dawning, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to look at the tomb.

note.traditional: In the end of the sabbath / After the Sabbath

verse.note: The Greek word usually means "late", which would give "late on the Sabbath". In this period it could also work as a preposition meaning "after". Most scholars take it that way here, since the next phrase places the scene at dawn on the first day of the week. A minority think Matthew reckons the day as ending at sunset, so that the scene is Saturday evening as the new day "draws on".

verse.text: And suddenly there was a great earthquake, for an angel of the Lord came down from heaven, approached, rolled away the stone, and sat on it.
His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing was white as snow.
The guards quaked for fear of him and became like dead men.
verse.note: The verb is the one from which the word for "earthquake" in verse 2 is formed. "Quaked" keeps the echo: the earth shakes, and so do the guards.

verse.text: But the angel said to the women, “As for you, do not be afraid, for I know that you are looking for Jesus, who was crucified.

text.q: He is not here, for he has been raised, just as he said. Come, see the place where he was lying.

verse.note: The Greek verb is passive in form. It can be read as a true passive ("he has been raised", with God as the implied agent) or as an intransitive ("he has risen"). Both are defensible. The passive is used here and in verse 7 because the New Testament regularly speaks of God raising Jesus.

text.q: Then go quickly and tell his disciples, ‘He has been raised from the dead, and look, he is going ahead of you to Galilee; there you will see him.’ Look, I have told you.”

verse.text: So they left the tomb quickly, with fear and great joy, and ran to tell his disciples.
And suddenly Jesus met them and said, “Greetings!” They came up, took hold of his feet, and bowed down before him.
verse.note: This was the ordinary everyday Greek greeting. Its literal sense is "rejoice", and some hear that overtone here after the "great joy" of verse 8. A first-century reader would have heard it first as a plain "hello".

The verb names a physical act: prostrating oneself before a superior, whether a king or a god. Here it accompanies grasping Jesus's feet. "Worshiped" is the traditional rendering, and many scholars think Matthew intends full religious devotion in this chapter, given the claim to all authority in verse 18. The rendering keeps the concrete gesture the Greek describes and leaves its significance to the context.

verse.text: Then Jesus said to them, “Do not be afraid. Go and tell my brothers to leave for Galilee, and there they will see me.”
While they were on their way, some of the guard went into the city and told the chief priests everything that had happened.
The chief priests met with the elders and, after forming a plan, gave the soldiers a large sum of silver,
telling them, “Say, ‘His disciples came by night and stole him while we were asleep.’

text.q: And if this comes to the governor’s ears, we will persuade him and see that you have nothing to worry about.”

verse.note: The Greek is literally "if this is heard before the governor". It may mean simply that the report reaches him, or more formally that the matter comes up for a hearing in his court. For a soldier, sleeping on watch was a serious offence, which is why the priests promise protection.

verse.text: So they took the silver and did as they had been instructed. And this story has been spread among Jews to this very day.
verse.note: The Greek has no article. It says the story circulated "among Jews", not that it was the view of "the Jews" as a whole. Most translations supply "the". Matthew, himself writing from within a Jewish setting, is describing a report current in his own day.

verse.text: The eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had directed them to go,
and when they saw him they bowed down before him, but some doubted.
verse.note: The Greek can be read as "but some doubted" (part of the group) or "but they doubted" (the same eleven who bowed down). Most translations take the first reading. The verb suggests hesitation or wavering rather than settled disbelief. Its only other New Testament use is of Peter on the water in Matthew 14:31.

verse.text: And Jesus came up and spoke to them, saying, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.

text.q: Go, therefore, and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,

verse.note: The same Greek word is translated "Gentiles" elsewhere, when the non-Jewish peoples are meant. Some scholars read this verse as "all the Gentiles", extending the earlier mission to Israel. Most take the phrase to mean all peoples without distinction, Israel included, and that is the reading followed here.

The Greek preposition is literally "into". Some scholars take the phrase to mean a transfer into the ownership or allegiance of the one named, a sense the expression can have in commercial documents of the period. Others note that "into" and "in" were often interchangeable in Greek of this period. The traditional "in the name" is kept, but the stronger sense is possible.

text.q: teaching them to keep all that I have commanded you. And look, I am with you all the days, until the end of the age.”

verse.note: The Greek says literally "all the days", a Semitic way of saying "always". It is kept because it completes a fourfold repetition in Jesus's closing words: all authority, all the nations, all that I have commanded, all the days.
